c-us6-ov-gdp.text: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series, in billions of chained 2017 dollars, real GDP was 1,191.1 in 1929, 1,089.8 in 1930, 1,020.0 in 1931, 888.4 in 1932, 877.4 in 1933, 972.3 in 1934, 1,058.8 in 1935, 1,195.3 in 1936, 1,256.5 in 1937, 1,214.9 in 1938, 1,312.4 in 1939, 1,428.1 in 1940, 1,681.0 in 1941, 1,998.5 in 1942, 2,338.8 in 1943, 2,524.8 in 1944 and 2,500.1 in 1945. Output fell about 26 percent from 1929 to 1933, was back above its 1929 level in 1936, and peaked in 1944 at more than twice the 1929 level.
c-us6-ov-gdp.label: approx
c-us6-ov-gdp.note: BEA's annual series begins in 1929. The percentage fall and the comparisons are this book's arithmetic.

c-us6-ov-mw.text: For the years before 1929, which BEA's series does not cover, MeasuringWorth's reconstruction puts real GDP at $841.4 billion in 1920, $822.1 billion in 1921 and $1,127.1 billion in 1928, in 2017 dollars: a rise of about 37 percent from 1921 to 1928.
c-us6-ov-mw.label: approx
c-us6-ov-mw.note: An academic reconstruction by Louis Johnston and Samuel Williamson; estimates before 1929 vary. It is a different series from BEA's, so its figures are not strictly comparable with BEA's figures for 1929 onward. The percentage is this book's arithmetic.

c-us6-ov-unemp.text: On Stanley Lebergott's annual estimates (NBER, 1957), unemployment was 11.9 percent in 1921 and 1.9 percent in 1926; from 1929 to 1945 it was 3.2, 8.9, 15.9, 23.6, 24.9 (the peak, 1933), 21.7, 20.1, 17.0, 14.3, 19.0, 17.2, 14.6, 9.9, 4.7, 1.9, 1.2 and 1.9 percent.
c-us6-ov-unemp.label: approx
c-us6-ov-unemp.note: Lebergott's annual averages (NBER, 1957); for 1929-39 his table takes the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates published in the Monthly Labor Review of July 1948. The series counts workers on New Deal emergency relief jobs as unemployed. Lebergott's later series (1964) and Michael Darby's alternative series, which counts relief workers as employed, are discussed in US6.5 and US6.7.

c-us6-ov-bls.text: Official unemployment figures for the 1930s were reconstructed afterwards: 'Estimates for the period 1929-39 were prepared by the Bureau of Labor Statistics', the Monthly Labor Review explained in 1948. They put the number unemployed in 1933 at 12,830,000.
c-us6-ov-bls.label: consensus

c-us6-ov-share.text: Federal net outlays were about 3.0 percent of GDP in 1929, 9.8 percent in 1934 and 40.7 percent in 1944.
c-us6-ov-share.label: approx
c-us6-ov-share.note: The series divides fiscal-year outlays by calendar-year GDP, so the two halves of the ratio cover slightly different periods.

c-us6-20s-ford.text: 'From 1908-1927, Ford Motor Company produced over 15 million Model T cars', and 'the price dropped from $850 to as little as $260.'
c-us6-20s-ford.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-line.text: 'Ford Motor Company began building magnetos on a crude moving assembly line in April 1913', at Highland Park. The moving line turned out 'a finished Model T every 93 minutes', against 12½ hours per car under stationary assembly.
c-us6-20s-line.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-elec.text: 'In 1907, only 8 percent of all dwellings were using electricity; by 1932, this figure had risen to 67 percent.' By 1932 more than 80 percent of urban dwellings had electric service, but only 11 percent of farm dwellings.
c-us6-20s-elec.label: approx
c-us6-20s-elec.note: The Energy Information Administration's round figures.

c-us6-20s-radio.text: KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the Harding-Cox election returns on 2 November 1920, and 'Within just four years of the initial KDKA broadcast, 600 stations existed in the U.S.'
c-us6-20s-radio.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-credit.text: Martha Olney's lecture notes put 70 to 90 percent of consumer durables in the 1920s as bought on instalments, and record that the ratio of consumer debt to income doubled during the decade. She is the author of Buy Now, Pay Later (1991).
c-us6-20s-credit.label: approx
c-us6-20s-credit.note: A range, not a single figure, from an economic historian's teaching notes.

c-us6-20s-olney.text: Martha Olney (1999) argues that households heavily in instalment debt cut other spending in 1930 to avoid defaulting, and that 'Consumer spending collapsed in 1930, turning a minor recession into the Great Depression.'
c-us6-20s-olney.label: debated
c-us6-20s-olney.note: One explanation of the slump among several; the others, including the monetary and gold-standard accounts, are set out in US6.5.

c-us6-20s-farm.text: In Minnesota, farm prices collapsed after the war: 'From 1919 to 1920, corn tumbled from $1.30 per bushel to forty-seven cents'.
c-us6-20s-farm.label: approx
c-us6-20s-farm.note: From MNopedia, a Minnesota reference work; these are Minnesota prices, not national ones, and are not checked here against national USDA series.

c-us6-20s-harding.text: Harding took office during a 'sharp deflation in 1920, which lasted for about one year', and signed the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921, which 'allowed the President to present a unified budget for the first time.'
c-us6-20s-harding.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-coolidge.text: 'Congress passed versions of the McNary-Haugen bill twice, but Coolidge vetoed them.' The bills were measures of farm relief.
c-us6-20s-coolidge.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-mellon.text: Under Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon the top income-tax rate fell from 73 percent to 58 percent under the Revenue Act of 1921, then to 46 percent in 1924 and to 25 percent in 1926.
c-us6-20s-mellon.label: consensus

c-us6-20s-mellondebate.text: Christopher Frenze's 1982 staff study for the Joint Economic Committee argues that the cuts raised revenue from the rich: 'Between 1921 and 1922', after the first cut, income taxes paid by those reporting incomes of $50,000 or more rose 'from $318 million to $446 million', an increase of over 40 percent. The Miller Center's essay on Coolidge says the cuts favoured the rich and that Coolidge's policies 'contributed to the stock market crash of 1929'. Gene Smiley and Richard Keehn (1995) note that the cuts 'have often been cited as an example of a successful supply-side policy' and also criticized as designed mainly to benefit the wealthy; they argue that a primary motive for them was to reduce tax avoidance by wealthier people, and that the cuts did reduce it.
c-us6-20s-mellondebate.label: debated
c-us6-20s-mellondebate.note: Three positions: a congressional staff study (Frenze, 1982), the Miller Center's presidential essay, whose author is not named in the page used here, and a peer-reviewed article (Smiley and Keehn, 1995). Frenze's revenue figures cover 1921-22 only, after the first cut. The three answer different questions: who paid the tax, whether Coolidge's policies fed the boom and crash, and why the rates were cut.

c-us6-20s-dow.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose from 63 in August 1921 until 'the index peaked on September 3, 1929, closing at 381.17'. Buyers on margin put down part of the price, 'typically 10 percent, and borrowed the rest.'
c-us6-20s-dow.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-18th.text: The Eighteenth Amendment prohibited 'the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors … for beverage purposes', to take effect 'After one year from the ratification of this article'. It was ratified on 16 January 1919.
c-us6-cult-18th.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-volstead.text: The Volstead Act of October 1919, which enforced Prohibition, defined intoxicating liquor as anything more than 0.5 percent alcohol. 'President Woodrow Wilson vetoes the Volstead Act... but Congress overrides his veto.'
c-us6-cult-volstead.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-miron.text: Jeffrey Miron and Jeffrey Zwiebel (1991) estimate that alcohol consumption 'fell sharply at the beginning of Prohibition, to approximately 30 percent' of its earlier level, then rose 'to about 60-70 percent of its pre-prohibition level'.
c-us6-cult-miron.label: approx
c-us6-cult-miron.note: Indirect estimates, built from mortality, mental-health and crime statistics rather than from records of sales.

c-us6-cult-21st.text: The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth and was ratified through conventions in the states. 'Utah became the 36th state to approve the 21st Amendment' on 5 December 1933, completing repeal.
c-us6-cult-21st.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-crime.text: In the ABA Journal's account, 'The rise of organized crime syndicates, spurred by a flourishing bootlegging industry' fed the movement for repeal.
c-us6-cult-crime.label: tradition
c-us6-cult-crime.note: A common account, as summarised by the ABA Journal; the sources used here do not weigh it against other reasons for repeal.

c-us6-cult-fosdick.text: In his sermon of 21 May 1922 at the First Presbyterian Church of New York, 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' (printed in The Christian Work on 10 June 1922), Harry Emerson Fosdick attacked the demand that Christians believe in the virgin birth and in a Bible God had 'inerrantly dictated to men a good deal as a man might dictate to a stenographer.'
c-us6-cult-fosdick.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-scopes.text: Tennessee's Butler Act made it unlawful 'to teach any theory that denies the story of divine creation as taught by the Bible'. Scopes's trial under it opened in Dayton on 10 July 1925; 'After 10 minutes' deliberation on July 21' the jury found him guilty.
c-us6-cult-scopes.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-bryan.text: Clarence Darrow questioned William Jennings Bryan, and 'Bryan was asked about a whale swallowing Jonah, Joshua making the sun stand still'. Bryan died days after the trial.
c-us6-cult-bryan.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-joshua.text: Joshua 10:13 in the NRSVUE reads: 'And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance on their enemies.'
c-us6-cult-joshua.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-appeal.text: On appeal, in January 1927, the Tennessee Supreme Court upheld the Butler Act as consistent with both the federal and the state constitutions, but set aside Scopes's conviction because of the way his fine had been set.
c-us6-cult-appeal.label: consensus

c-us6-cult-klan.text: Estimates of the 1920s Klan's membership differ. Scott McLemee, reviewing Linda Gordon's The Second Coming of the KKK in Inside Higher Ed (2017), notes that 'At its peak, the Klan claimed to have four to six million members or more'. Gordon told TIME in 2017: 'At its peak, the Klan numbered between 3 million and 5 million people in the North'. McLemee argues that the claimed figure is credible only if it includes four or five million who signed up and quit after a couple of meetings; 'If so, that would leave a million members'.
c-us6-cult-klan.label: debated
c-us6-cult-klan.note: The highest figure is the Klan's own claim. Gordon's figure, given in an interview, is for the North at the peak. McLemee's million follows from his assumption that most recruits soon quit, so part of the gap lies between everyone who ever joined and membership at any one time.

c-us6-cult-indiana.text: The publisher's description of Leonard Moore's Citizen Klansmen says that more than 25 percent of native-born men in Indiana became official members of the Klan. The History Museum in South Bend puts the figure at 250,000 white men, about 30 percent of the state's native-born white men, and records that Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson was convicted of second-degree murder in the death of Madge Oberholtzer.
c-us6-cult-indiana.label: approx
c-us6-cult-indiana.note: Two round figures for Indiana, from Moore's publisher and from a local museum; neither counts members at a single date.

c-us6-imm-1921.text: 'On May 19, 1921, President Warren Harding signed the Quota Act of 1921.' It admitted each year 3 percent of the foreign-born of each nationality counted in the 1910 census, about 350,000 people a year, and 'did not, however, establish quotas of any kind for residents of the Western Hemisphere'.
c-us6-imm-1921.label: consensus

c-us6-imm-1924.text: The Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 cut the quota to 2 percent and 'pushed back the year on which quota calculations were based from 1910 to 1890'. 'The 1924 law capped quota immigration at 164,667 people per year'; under the national-origins system, from 1929, the cap was 153,879.
c-us6-imm-1924.label: consensus

c-us6-imm-asia.text: The 1924 act barred aliens ineligible for citizenship, which 'completely excluded immigrants from Asia'. 'The Japanese government protested, but the law remained.'
c-us6-imm-asia.label: consensus

c-us6-imm-sacco.text: Sacco and Vanzetti were tried in 1921 for a payroll robbery and murder and were executed on 23 August 1927. In 1977 Governor Michael Dukakis of Massachusetts proclaimed that 'any stigma and disgrace' should be removed from their names, declaring that 'The atmosphere of their trial and appeals was permeated by prejudice against foreigners'.
c-us6-imm-sacco.label: consensus

c-us6-imm-saccoguilt.text: Whether they were guilty is still disputed. Douglas Linder's account reports that a ballistics test in 1961 gave 'strong evidence that Sacco did indeed fire a fatal bullet', and that some argue one of the two men may have been guilty and the other innocent.
c-us6-imm-saccoguilt.label: debated
c-us6-imm-saccoguilt.note: The unfairness of the trial is widely accepted, and Dukakis's proclamation states it; the men's guilt is not settled. Linder's account sets the 1961 ballistics evidence against the view that both were innocent.

c-us6-imm-repat.text: Scholars' estimates of Mexican repatriation in the 1930s differ. As summarised by Lee, Peri and Yasenov, Hoffman (1974) put the number at 400,000 to 500,000; Gratton and Merchant (2013), with Hoffman, imply about 400,000; and Balderrama and Rodríguez (2006) put it as high as one million. Lee, Peri and Yasenov (2022), who write that the lower figures fit the census data better, describe an episode in which 'at least 400,000 Mexicans returned to Mexico between 1929 and 1934'.
c-us6-imm-repat.label: debated
c-us6-imm-repat.note: Hoffman's, Gratton and Merchant's and Balderrama and Rodríguez's figures are given here only as Lee, Peri and Yasenov summarise them. The 400,000 is background to their study, which they credit to 'the most reasonable estimates', not a count of their own; their own result concerns labour markets. The estimates cover different periods.

c-us6-imm-calif.text: California's Apology Act of 2005 (Government Code section 8721) states that 'it is estimated that two million people of Mexican ancestry were forcibly relocated', 'approximately 1.2 million of whom had been born in the United States'.
c-us6-imm-calif.label: debated
c-us6-imm-calif.note: This is the legislature's figure, stated in a statute, not a scholarly estimate; the scholarly estimates summarised by Lee, Peri and Yasenov run from about 400,000 to one million.

c-us6-imm-lpylabor.text: Lee, Peri and Yasenov (2022) find that 'Mexican repatriations resulted in reduced employment and occupational downgrading for U.S. natives.'
c-us6-imm-lpylabor.label: debated
c-us6-imm-lpylabor.note: A new finding (2022) by one research team, using longitudinal data from the 1930s; it runs against the idea that removing Mexican workers would open jobs for natives.

c-us6-black-migration.text: 'From World War I until World War II, it is estimated that about 2 million Black people left the South', according to the National Archives; 'Between 1910 and 1970, an estimated 6 million Blacks left the South', according to the Census Bureau.
c-us6-black-migration.label: approx
c-us6-black-migration.note: Both are estimates, for different periods, from two federal agencies.

c-us6-black-tulsa.text: On 31 May and 1 June 1921 a mob destroyed 35 blocks of Tulsa's Greenwood district and about 1,256 homes.
c-us6-black-tulsa.label: consensus

c-us6-black-toll.text: Oklahoma's commission, reporting on 28 February 2001, judged that the dead were 'likely numbering between one and three hundred'. It reported that its forensic anthropologist, Clyde Snow, could identify thirty-eight victims 'By the most conservative of all possible methods'.
c-us6-black-toll.label: approx
c-us6-black-toll.note: The commission's range is an estimate; 38 is the minimum Snow could identify, not a total. The words quoted are the commission's, summarising Snow's work.

c-us6-black-doj.text: The Justice Department's review, announced on 10 January 2025, called the massacre 'a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood'. It found that some police took part in 'murder, arson and looting', but that there was 'no living perpetrator' who could be prosecuted.
c-us6-black-doj.label: consensus

c-us6-black-court.text: In June 2024 the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed the survivors' suit, brought under Oklahoma's public nuisance law. Randle's lawyer said on 30 May 2026: 'Unfortunately our litigation was ended back in 2024'.
c-us6-black-court.label: consensus

c-us6-black-survivors.text: Viola Fletcher, a survivor of the massacre, died at 111 (KGOU, 24 November 2025). Lessie Benningfield Randle was alive on 6 October 2026: 'At 111 years old, Mother Lessie Benningfield Randle'.
c-us6-black-survivors.label: consensus

c-us6-black-trust.text: On 1 June 2025 Tulsa's mayor, Monroe Nichols, presented a plan called the Road to Repair, under which 'the Greenwood Trust will be created with the goal to secure $105 million in assets', 'with most of the funding secured, or committed, by June 1, 2026'.
c-us6-black-trust.label: approx
c-us6-black-trust.note: A goal stated by the city in 2025, not a result; this book has not confirmed how much had been secured or committed by June 2026.

c-us6-black-harlem.text: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2024) treats the Harlem Renaissance as part of 'the new Black cities that took shape in the 1920s–40s'. Its artists included Aaron Douglas, Augusta Savage and James Van Der Zee.
c-us6-black-harlem.label: consensus

c-us6-black-garvey.text: Marcus Garvey co-founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in 1914 and arrived in Harlem in 1916. His trial for mail fraud began on 18 May 1923, and on 21 June he was sentenced to five years in prison; his sentence was commuted, and in 1927 he 'is deported from the U. S., never to return'. He died in London in 1940. President Biden pardoned him posthumously on 19 January 2025.
c-us6-black-garvey.label: consensus

c-us6-black-scottsboro.text: On 25 March 1931 nine Black youths, aged 13 to 19 by Prologue's account (the Encyclopedia of Alabama gives 13 to 20), were seized at Paint Rock, Alabama, and taken to Scottsboro, the Jackson County seat, where they were first tried in April 1931. Their defence was run by the International Labor Defense (ILD), 'the legal arm of the Communist Party'. One accuser, Ruby Bates, recanted and testified for the defence at Haywood Patterson's second trial in 1933 that there had been no rape (as reported by Prologue).
c-us6-black-scottsboro.label: consensus

c-us6-black-powell.text: In Powell v. Alabama (7 November 1932) the Supreme Court held that the failure to provide effective counsel in a capital case was 'a denial of due process within the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment'. In Norris v. Alabama (1 April 1935) it held that evidence that no Black citizen had been called for jury service 'for a generation or longer' 'established the discrimination which the Constitution forbids', a denial of equal protection.
c-us6-black-powell.label: consensus

c-us6-black-pardon.text: On 21 November 2013 Alabama posthumously pardoned 'Charles Weems, Andy Wright, and Haywood Patterson'.
c-us6-black-pardon.label: consensus

c-us6-crash-dow.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at 381.17 on 3 September 1929. On Black Monday, 28 October 1929, it fell nearly 13 percent, and on 29 October nearly 12 percent more. It bottomed at 41.22 in the summer of 1932, 89 percent below its peak, and regained its 1929 high only in November 1954.
c-us6-crash-dow.label: consensus

c-us6-crash-romer.text: A recession had begun in the summer of 1929, before the crash. Christina Romer argues that the crash deepened it, chiefly by cutting purchases of durable goods: 'The stock market crash is the prime source for the collapse in durable goods purchases starting in November 1929.'
c-us6-crash-romer.label: consensus

c-us6-crash-gdp.text: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis series, real GDP fell from $1,191.1 billion in 1929 to $877.4 billion in 1933, in chained 2017 dollars, a fall of about 26 percent between the annual averages. Britannica, measuring 'Between the peak and the trough of the downturn', states that 'real gross domestic product (GDP) fell 30 percent'.
c-us6-crash-gdp.label: approx
c-us6-crash-gdp.note: Two measures: about 26 percent between the annual averages of 1929 and 1933 in the BEA's series (as published on FRED), and 30 percent from peak to trough in Britannica. This book therefore says 'about a quarter to 30 percent, depending on the measure'; the charts use the BEA series.

c-us6-crash-ip.text: Britannica states that 'industrial production in the United States declined 47 percent'; Romer finds that producer prices fell by slightly over 40 percent between July 1929 and July 1932.
c-us6-crash-ip.label: approx
c-us6-crash-ip.note: Peak-to-trough estimates from two sources, measured over slightly different periods.

c-us6-crash-banks.text: The FDIC states that 'about 9,000 banks suspended operations, resulting in losses to depositors of about $1.3 billion.' The Social Security Administration's history page states: 'In all, 9,000 banks failed--taking with them $7 billion in depositors' assets.'
c-us6-crash-banks.label: approx
c-us6-crash-banks.note: The two dollar figures measure different things. The FDIC's $1.3 billion is what depositors lost; the SSA's $7 billion is the depositors' money held in the banks that failed, not net losses. Both sources count about 9,000 failed or suspended banks.

c-us6-crash-panics.text: Banking panics came in waves: the Caldwell banks, based in Nashville, failed in November 1930; on 11 December 1930 the Bank of United States, the fourth-largest bank in New York City, ceased operations; and a banking crisis struck Chicago in June 1931.
c-us6-crash-panics.label: consensus

c-us6-crash-money.text: From the fall of 1930 to the winter of 1933, 'the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent.'
c-us6-crash-money.label: consensus

c-us6-crash-unemp.text: In the standard series of Lebergott (1957; 1964) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which for 1929-39 use the same BLS estimates, unemployment peaked in 1933 at 24.9 percent. Michael Darby, in an NBER working paper of May 1975, reported 'A major conceptual error in the standard BLS and Lebergott unemployment estimates for 1933-1943': they counted workers on federal emergency relief projects as unemployed. Counting them as employed, Darby gives 24.3 and 24.0 percent for 1933 (dividing by Lebergott's and by the BLS labor force), but 10.1 percent instead of 17.0 for 1936 and 11.3 instead of 17.2 for 1939.
c-us6-crash-unemp.label: debated
c-us6-crash-unemp.note: A dispute about definitions, not about the count. Lebergott and the BLS treat people on work-relief projects such as the WPA as unemployed; Darby treats them as employed. The choice changes the rates from 1933 on, so it matters which series a writer quotes. Darby's figures here are those of his 1975 working paper; the published version (Journal of Political Economy, 1976) differs (see US6.7).

c-us6-crash-series.text: Table 3 of Darby's NBER working paper (May 1975) gives, in percent, the unemployment rate with relief workers counted as unemployed (Darby's own calculation: the BLS-Lebergott count of the unemployed divided by Lebergott's civilian labor force) and Darby's corrected rate on the same base: 1929 3.2 and 3.2; 1930 8.9 and 8.9; 1931 16.3 and 16.3; 1932 24.1 and 24.1; 1933 25.2 and 24.3; 1934 22.0 and 17.2; 1935 20.3 and 15.4; 1936 17.0 and 10.1; 1937 14.3 and 9.3; 1938 19.1 and 12.5; 1939 17.2 and 11.3; 1940 14.6 and 9.6; 1941 9.9 and 6.0.
c-us6-crash-series.label: approx
c-us6-crash-series.note: Annual estimates. The two series differ only in how relief workers are counted. Because Darby divides by Lebergott's labor force, his uncorrected rates run slightly above the rates Lebergott and the BLS published (25.2 against 24.9 percent for 1933; 24.1 against 23.6 for 1932). Darby's footnote says that his 1933 figure still counts the substantial number of state and local work-relief recipients as unemployed. Robert Margo's Table 1 (1993), which takes the rates from Smiley (1983), gives Darby's published (1976) rate as 20.6 percent for 1933 and 9.9 for 1936, against Lebergott's 24.9 and 16.9.

c-us6-crash-fs.text: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, in A Monetary History of the United States, argued, as their publisher summarises the book, that the Federal Reserve failed to exercise its role of managing the monetary system and countering banking panics.
c-us6-crash-fs.label: debated
c-us6-crash-fs.note: The monetary explanation. Peter Temin (1976) challenged it, stressing a fall in spending; Eichengreen, Temin and Sachs place the slump in the setting of the gold standard; Bernanke adds a credit channel. Given here in the publisher's summary, not the authors' words.

c-us6-crash-temin.text: Peter Temin, in Did Monetary Forces Cause the Great Depression? (1976), concludes, as Kirkus Reviews reports, that 'there is no evidence that the banking panic of 1930 had a deflationary effect on the economy', and that the data are 'consistent with the spending hypothesis', the view that a fall in spending caused the slump.
c-us6-crash-temin.label: debated
c-us6-crash-temin.note: The spending explanation, set against Friedman and Schwartz's monetary one. Known here only through a review, which quotes his conclusion. Temin also wrote with Eichengreen on the gold standard.

c-us6-crash-gold.text: Barry Eichengreen and Peter Temin argue that 'the mentality of the gold standard was pervasive and compelling to the leaders of the interwar economy.' Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs found that 'currency depreciation was beneficial for the initiating countries.'
c-us6-crash-gold.label: debated
c-us6-crash-gold.note: The gold-standard explanation, from the authors' NBER abstracts; on the gold standard worldwide see 15.4. Friedman and Schwartz stress the Federal Reserve, Temin (1976) spending and Bernanke credit; the debate is over how much weight each deserves.

c-us6-crash-bernanke.text: Ben Bernanke (1983) argued that 'the financial disruptions of 1930-33 reduced the efficiency of the credit allocation process.' Awarding him a share of the 2022 economics prize, the Nobel committee wrote that 'he showed how bank runs were a decisive factor in the crisis becoming so deep and prolonged.'
c-us6-crash-bernanke.label: debated
c-us6-crash-bernanke.note: The importance of the credit channel is widely accepted, as the 2022 prize shows; how much of the slump it explains, compared with the money supply (Friedman and Schwartz) or spending (Temin), is still debated.

c-us6-crash-tariff.text: The Office of the Historian notes that historians debate whether the Tariff Act of 1930 (Smoot-Hawley) provoked 'a wave of foreign retaliation that plunged the world deeper into the Great Depression.'
c-us6-crash-tariff.label: debated
c-us6-crash-tariff.note: The tariff's existence is not in doubt; its effect is. Some historians see it as provoking damaging retaliation, others doubt that it did.

c-us6-nd1-rfc.text: President Hoover signed the Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act on 22 January 1932. The RFC, with $500 million in capital, lent to banks and other financial institutions, insurance companies and railroads, and from July 1932 to states and cities.
c-us6-nd1-rfc.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-inaug.text: In his first inaugural address, on 4 March 1933, Franklin D. Roosevelt said, in the American Presidency Project's transcript of the speech as delivered (which differs slightly from the text as prepared): 'So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.' He also said: 'Yes, the money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization', and 'Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.' He asked for 'broad Executive power to wage a war against the emergency'.
c-us6-nd1-inaug.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-holiday.text: Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday by Proclamation 2039 on 6 March 1933; Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act on 9 March; banks began to reopen on 13 March, and by 15 March banks holding 90 percent of the system's resources had reopened. But 'some 4,000 banks would remain closed forever.'
c-us6-nd1-holiday.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-gs.text: The Banking Act of 1933 (Glass-Steagall), signed on 16 June 1933, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and 'effectively separated commercial banking from investment banking.' The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 repealed its limits on affiliations between the two.
c-us6-nd1-gs.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-gold.text: On 20 April 1933 the gold standard was suspended; on 5 June gold clauses in contracts were abrogated; and the Gold Reserve Act, signed on 30 January 1934, authorized the president to set the gold value of the dollar by proclamation, which Roosevelt did the next day, at $35 an ounce, up from $20.67. Federal Reserve History states: 'Scholars believe Roosevelt's reflation accelerated America's recovery from the Great Depression.'
c-us6-nd1-gold.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-aaa.text: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of May 1933 paid farmers to cut production, aiming to restore farm purchasing power to its level of 1909-14. 'The U.S. Supreme Court declared the act unconstitutional in 1936.'
c-us6-nd1-aaa.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-nira.text: The National Industrial Recovery Act of 16 June 1933 set up industry codes of fair competition; its Section 7(a) provided that 'employees shall have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing', and its Title II funded public works.
c-us6-nd1-nira.label: consensus

c-us6-nd1-ccc.text: The Civilian Conservation Corps was created by executive order on 5 April 1933. Enrollees earned $30 a month, $25 of which was sent home; there were 1,433 camps by July 1933. Minorities were enrolled, in the National Park Service's words, 'at far lower rates than the legislation allowed'. The CCC ended in 1942.
c-us6-nd1-ccc.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-wpa.text: The Works Progress Administration, created in 1935, put some 8.5 million people to work at a cost of about $11 billion before it ended in 1943.
c-us6-nd2-wpa.label: approx
c-us6-nd2-wpa.note: Britannica's round figures for the whole life of the programme.

c-us6-nd2-excl.text: Larry DeWitt, a historian at the Social Security Administration, writes that the 1935 Social Security Act 'excluded from coverage about half the workers in the American economy', among them agricultural and domestic workers, and that 65 percent of African American workers fell outside it; '27 percent of the white workforce was likewise excluded from coverage.'
c-us6-nd2-excl.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-katz.text: Ira Katznelson, in When Affirmative Action Was White (2005), stresses the power of southern members of Congress over the shape of New Deal laws; as a Columbia Magazine review summarises his argument, the New Deal in effect traded away the interests of Black Americans to win major benefits for whites. DeWitt lists Robert Lieberman and Linda Gordon among other scholars who see a racial motive in the exclusions.
c-us6-nd2-katz.label: debated
c-us6-nd2-katz.note: One side of the debate over motive: Katznelson, Lieberman, Gordon and others see the exclusions as shaped by racial politics. DeWitt (2010) disagrees. Katznelson's own text was not opened; his view is given as a reviewer summarises it.

c-us6-nd2-dewitt.text: DeWitt argues that 'the racial-bias thesis is both conceptually flawed and unsupported', and that the exclusion 'was due to considerations of administrative feasibility involving tax-collection procedures.'
c-us6-nd2-dewitt.label: debated
c-us6-nd2-dewitt.note: The other side of the debate over motive. DeWitt accepts that the exclusions fell heavily on Black workers; he disputes that race was the reason for them.

c-us6-nd2-wagner.text: The National Labor Relations Act (the Wagner Act), signed on 5 July 1935, gave employees the right, under Section 7, to form and join unions, required employers to bargain with unions chosen by a majority of workers, and created the National Labor Relations Board.
c-us6-nd2-wagner.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-flsa.text: The Fair Labor Standards Act, signed on 25 June 1938 after the House passed it by 291 to 89, set a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and a 44-hour week at first, and banned oppressive child labor. It applied only to industries whose combined employment was about one-fifth of the labor force.
c-us6-nd2-flsa.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-schechter.text: In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (27 May 1935) a unanimous Court, in an opinion by Chief Justice Hughes, with Justice Cardozo concurring, ruled against the National Industrial Recovery Act's code system. Hughes wrote: 'Extraordinary conditions do not create or enlarge constitutional power'.
c-us6-nd2-schechter.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-court.text: On 5 February 1937 Roosevelt proposed to add one justice for each sitting justice over the age of 70, up to six. The Senate Judiciary Committee called the plan 'an invasion of judicial power such as has never before been attempted in this country', and it was shelved by July 1937.
c-us6-nd2-court.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-wch.text: In West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish (29 March 1937) the Court, by 5 to 4, upheld a minimum-wage law and overruled Adkins (1923). Chief Justice Hughes wrote: 'The Constitution does not speak of freedom of contract.'
c-us6-nd2-wch.label: consensus

c-us6-nd2-switch.text: Whether Justice Owen Roberts changed his vote in West Coast Hotel because of the court-packing plan is debated; the National Constitution Center notes that historians also point to other legal reasoning. The 'switch in time' reading, which William Leuchtenburg describes as the view of contemporaries, ties the decision to the plan. G. Edward White (2012) points out that 'the Justices' conference on West Coast Hotel had taken place on December 19, 1936', that Roberts voted there to sustain the Washington statute, and that the plan was first introduced in February 1937; he concludes that Roberts's switch 'had nothing to do with the introduction of the Court-packing plan'.
c-us6-nd2-switch.label: debated
c-us6-nd2-switch.note: Two readings: the traditional one, which White says became orthodoxy and which he illustrates from Leuchtenburg, and the internal, doctrinal one that White argues. Leuchtenburg is given here as White presents him.

c-us6-eval-gdp.text: In the BEA series (billions of chained 2017 dollars), real GDP was 1,191.1 in 1929, 877.4 in 1933, 972.3 in 1934, 1,058.8 in 1935, 1,195.3 in 1936, 1,256.5 in 1937, 1,214.9 in 1938, 1,312.4 in 1939, 1,428.1 in 1940 and 1,681.0 in 1941: it passed its 1929 level in 1936 and grew about 43 percent from 1933 to 1937. Britannica writes that 'real GDP rose at an average rate of 9 percent per year between 1933 and 1937.'
c-us6-eval-gdp.label: consensus

c-us6-eval-1937.text: A recession ran from May 1937 to June 1938: real GDP fell 10 percent, industrial production 32 percent, and unemployment rose back to 20 percent. Federal Reserve History lists among its causes that 'Fed policymakers doubled reserve requirement ratios to soak up banks' excess reserves', the Treasury's sterilization of gold inflows, the new Social Security payroll tax and tighter fiscal policy.
c-us6-eval-1937.label: debated
c-us6-eval-1937.note: The events are agreed; how much weight each cause deserves is debated. The 10 percent fall is measured from peak to trough within the years; the annual BEA figures show a fall of 3.3 percent from 1937 to 1938.

c-us6-eval-romer.text: Christina Romer argues that 'nearly all of the observed recovery of the U.S. economy prior to 1942 was due to monetary expansion', fed by 'Huge gold inflows'.
c-us6-eval-romer.label: debated
c-us6-eval-romer.note: From her NBER abstract. On this view fiscal policy did little before the war; Cole and Ohanian and their critics argue instead about the New Deal's other policies.

c-us6-eval-co.text: Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian (2004) conclude that 'New Deal cartelization policies are an important factor in accounting for the failure of the economy to recover back to trend.'
c-us6-eval-co.label: debated
c-us6-eval-co.note: Contested: Gauti Eggertsson (2012) argues that in the conditions of the 1930s such policies were expansionary.

c-us6-eval-egg.text: Gauti Eggertsson (2012) argues that when interest rates are at zero and prices are falling, policies that increase the monopoly power of firms and the militancy of unions, such as the New Deal policies that Cole and Ohanian criticize, can increase output: 'These emergency conditions--zero interest rates and deflation--were satisfied during the Great Depression', and the New Deal 'was therefore expansionary in the model presented'.
c-us6-eval-egg.label: debated
c-us6-eval-egg.note: A direct answer to Cole and Ohanian, who find that the same policies held recovery back.

c-us6-eval-fk.text: Price Fishback and Valentina Kachanovskaya (2015) find that a dollar of federal spending in a state raised its per capita income 'by between 40 and 96 cents', but had 'no positive effects on private employment.'
c-us6-eval-fk.label: debated
c-us6-eval-fk.note: A range of estimates from state-level data. Romer credits monetary expansion, not federal spending, for the recovery.

c-us6-eval-survey.text: In a survey of the research, Fishback finds that relief and public works spending had state income multipliers 'of around one', 'reduced crime rates, and lowered several types of mortality'; that the farm programs 'typically aided large farm owners but eliminated opportunities for share croppers, tenants, and farm workers'; and that the HOLC 'staved off drops in housing prices and home ownership rates'.
c-us6-eval-survey.label: approx
c-us6-eval-survey.note: A survey of many studies; the estimates vary by programme.

c-us6-eval-ahm.text: Daniel Aaronson, Daniel Hartley and Bhashkar Mazumder (2021) find that the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's 1930s maps, which marked some neighborhoods in red, had lasting effects: 'The maps led to reduced home ownership rates, house values, and rents' and 'increased racial segregation in later decades.'
c-us6-eval-ahm.label: debated
c-us6-eval-ahm.note: Contested by Fishback, Rose, Snowden and Storrs (2021-24), who argue that the HOLC's maps had little effect on where the HOLC and the FHA lent, and that the FHA's redlining came first.

c-us6-eval-frss.text: Price Fishback, Jonathan Rose, Kenneth Snowden and Thomas Storrs (2021; 2024) argue that the Federal Housing Administration redlined first, that 'the HOLC itself broadly loaned to such neighborhoods and to Black homeowners', and that 'the HOLC's redlining maps had little effect on the geographic distribution of either program's mortgage market activity'. In a Chicago Fed policy brief (April 2022), Jonathan Rose, one of the co-authors, concludes that 'the red lines drawn by the FHA were likely far more impactful than the HOLC's.'
c-us6-eval-frss.label: debated
c-us6-eval-frss.note: New work, set against Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder (2021). The Chicago Fed brief is by one of the paper's own authors, so it restates their case rather than confirming it independently. The two sides differ on whether the HOLC's maps did lasting damage, and on the FHA's role.

c-us6-faith-dust.text: Strictly, the Dust Bowl covered western Kansas, southeastern Colorado and the Oklahoma Panhandle, with adjoining areas. Droughts struck in 1930-31, 1934, 1936 and 1939-40. Low crop prices, pushed lower by a record wheat crop in 1931, and high machinery costs led farmers to put more submarginal land into production, while the one-way disc plow 'greatly increased the risk of blowing soil'.
c-us6-faith-dust.label: consensus

c-us6-faith-black.text: On Black Sunday, 14 April 1935, a dust storm hit Boise City, Oklahoma, at about 5:15 pm. The National Weather Service writes: 'It is generally established that the term 'Dust Bowl' originated from the events of Black Sunday', in an Associated Press report published in the Lubbock Evening Journal the next day, 15 April 1935.
c-us6-faith-black.label: consensus

c-us6-faith-okies.text: James Gregory estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 people from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and Missouri settled in California in the 1930s, and writes that 'The actual Dust Bowl counties were sparsely populated and contributed few refugees.'
c-us6-faith-okies.label: approx
c-us6-faith-okies.note: Gregory's estimate, given as a range.

c-us6-faith-long.text: Huey Long's Share Our Wealth plan, as set out in the Congressional Record in 1934-35, proposed to limit fortunes to 'not more than $3 to 4 million'; that every family should 'possess not less than $5,000 free of debt'; an income 'of not less than $2,500 per year to every family'; and 'Old-age pensions of $30 per month to persons over 60 years of age'.
c-us6-faith-long.label: consensus

c-us6-faith-coughlin.text: Charles Coughlin, a Catholic priest at the Shrine of the Little Flower in Royal Oak, Michigan, had a regular radio audience that the US Holocaust Memorial Museum puts at 30 million. In 1933 he hailed the New Deal as Christ's Deal; already in February 1933, the museum records, he had attacked bankers as 'modern Shylocks', a phrase that drew on antisemitic stereotypes. In his broadcast of 20 November 1938, 'Persecution—Jewish and Christian', ten days after Kristallnacht, he claimed that Jews controlled the radio and the press and blamed Jewish communism; in 1938 his magazine Social Justice serialized the antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. In 1941 Archbishop Edward Mooney ordered him to stop broadcasting, and on 1 May 1942 Mooney instructed him to stop engaging in non-pastoral activities or risk being defrocked.
c-us6-faith-coughlin.label: approx
c-us6-faith-coughlin.note: The audience figure is an estimate. His antisemitism is not in dispute; it is described here as the museum describes it, since the full broadcast texts were not opened.

c-us6-faith-qa.text: In Quadragesimo Anno (15 May 1931) Pope Pius XI taught that 'the worker must be paid a wage sufficient to support him and his family' (para. 71); stated the principle of subsidiarity, 'Just as it is gravely wrong to take from individuals what they can accomplish by their own initiative and industry and give it to the community, so also it is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do' (para. 79); and declared that 'no one can be at the same time a good Catholic and a true socialist' (para. 120).
c-us6-faith-qa.label: consensus

c-us6-faith-cw.text: The Catholic Worker was founded in New York City in 1933 by Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin. The movement ran houses of hospitality that welcomed the poor as guests rather than as clients.
c-us6-faith-cw.label: consensus

c-us6-faith-best.text: The historian Wallace Best describes how Black migrants in Chicago flocked to storefront churches; the church of Elder Lucy Smith fed as many as about 90 people a day, and Best found no mainline Black church giving such relief.
c-us6-faith-best.label: approx
c-us6-faith-best.note: One historian's findings, given in an interview; the figure for meals is approximate.

c-us6-faith-divine.text: Father Divine's Peace Mission Movement served food at very low prices and was racially integrated.
c-us6-faith-divine.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-acts.text: 'On August 31, 1935, Congress passed the first Neutrality Act', which banned the export of arms to nations at war. A law of 1936 added a ban on loans to belligerents, and one of 1937 allowed the president to let belligerents buy goods other than arms on a 'cash-and-carry' basis.
c-us6-neut-acts.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-1939.text: The Neutrality Act of November 1939 lifted the arms embargo and put all trade with belligerents on a cash-and-carry basis; American ships were barred from belligerent ports, and 'The ban on loans remained in effect.'
c-us6-neut-1939.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-afc.text: The America First Committee (1940-41), which opposed American entry into the war, 'claimed a membership of 800,000'; it dissolved after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
c-us6-neut-afc.label: approx
c-us6-neut-afc.note: The membership figure is the committee's own claim.

c-us6-neut-lindbergh.text: At an America First rally in Des Moines on 11 September 1941, 'Lindbergh accused Great Britain, Jews, and the Roosevelt administration of leading the United States into war.'
c-us6-neut-lindbergh.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-stlouis.text: The St. Louis left Hamburg on 13 May 1939 with 937 passengers; Cuba, the United States and Canada refused to admit them, and 'Ultimately, 254 St. Louis passengers were killed in the Holocaust.'
c-us6-neut-stlouis.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-wagner.text: The Wagner-Rogers bill, introduced on 9 February 1939, would have permitted 'the entry of 20,000 refugee children, ages 14 and under' over two years; it 'died in the Senate Immigration Committee during the first week of July 1939.'
c-us6-neut-wagner.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-quotas.text: The quotas were treated as ceilings: from 1933 to 1941 'roughly 118,000 German quota slots that could have been used went unfilled.' The German quota after 1929 was 25,957 a year, and from July 1941 visa control was centralized in Washington.
c-us6-neut-quotas.label: approx

c-us6-neut-lendlease.text: Lend-Lease, 'An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States', was 'Approved, March 11, 1941.' The program eventually dispensed 'some $50 billion in assistance'.
c-us6-neut-lendlease.label: approx
c-us6-neut-lendlease.note: The total is the Office of the Historian's round figure ('some').

c-us6-neut-atlantic.text: Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard USS Augusta in Placentia Bay on 9-10 August 1941, and their joint declaration of eight principles, the Atlantic Charter, was released on 14 August. It begins: 'First, their countries seek no aggrandizement, territorial or other'; and the third principle reads: 'Third, they respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live'.
c-us6-neut-atlantic.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-infamy.text: On 8 December 1941 Roosevelt told a joint session of Congress: 'Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.' He closed: 'I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.'
c-us6-neut-infamy.label: consensus

c-us6-neut-draft.text: Roosevelt's draft of the address read 'a date which will live in world history'.
c-us6-neut-draft.label: consensus

c-us6-home-gdp.text: Real GDP rose from $1,312 billion in 1939 to $2,525 billion in 1944, in chained 2017 dollars, an increase of about 92 percent; it was $2,500 billion in 1945 and $2,210 billion in 1946.
c-us6-home-gdp.label: approx
c-us6-home-gdp.note: Annual estimates of the Bureau of Economic Analysis, in 'Billions of Chained 2017 Dollars', as published on FRED; the percentage is computed from them.

c-us6-home-fiscal.text: Federal net outlays rose from 9.8 percent of GDP in fiscal 1939 to 40.7 percent in fiscal 1944 and 1945, and fell to 24.3 percent in 1946. Federal debt held by the public was 44.3 percent of GDP in 1939, 37.3 percent in 1941 and 103.2 percent in 1945. Year by year (outlays; debt): 1940, 9.2 and 41.6; 1941, 10.6 and 37.3; 1942, 21.2 and 40.9; 1943, 38.7 and 62.9; 1944, 40.7 and 82.3; 1945, 40.7 and 103.2; 1946, 24.3 and 106.3.
c-us6-home-fiscal.label: approx
c-us6-home-fiscal.note: Ratios constructed by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis from OMB and BEA data, as published on FRED, by fiscal year.

c-us6-home-women.text: The Women's Bureau reported in 1946 that women's employment 'increased almost 60 percent between 1940 and 1945'.
c-us6-home-women.label: approx
c-us6-home-women.note: A rounded figure from the Women's Bureau's own count ('almost').

c-us6-home-rose.text: Evan K. Rose (Journal of Economic History, 2018) uses new data on wartime employment and job placements. He argues that where women took wartime jobs was driven mainly by industrial mobilization rather than by drafted men leaving local labor markets, and that the areas most exposed to wartime work show 'limited overall effects on female labor force participation in 1950'.
c-us6-home-rose.label: debated
c-us6-home-rose.note: Rose's reading questions the view that wartime work lastingly raised women's employment; it rests on one study's new data.

c-us6-home-doublev.text: In a letter to the Pittsburgh Courier dated 31 January 1942, James G. Thompson proposed: 'let we colored Americans adopt the double VV for a double victory.' 'Locked out of jobs on the factory floor', as the National Park Service puts it, 'Thompson worked in the cafeteria at Cessna.'
c-us6-home-doublev.label: consensus

c-us6-home-eo9066.text: Executive Order 9066, signed on 19 February 1942, 'authorized the forced removal of all persons deemed a threat to national security'. About 122,000 people of Japanese ancestry were removed, nearly 70,000 of them American citizens, and held in ten incarceration centers.
c-us6-home-eo9066.label: approx

c-us6-home-korematsu.text: In Korematsu v. United States, decided on 18 December 1944, the Court upheld the exclusion order by six votes to three. Justice Hugo Black wrote for the Court that courts 'must subject them to the most rigid scrutiny', speaking of legal restrictions on a single racial group. Justice Frank Murphy, dissenting, called the decision 'this legalization of racism', and Justice Robert Jackson warned that its principle 'lies about like a loaded weapon'.
c-us6-home-korematsu.label: consensus

c-us6-home-redress.text: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-383) found that the incarceration was 'motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership', apologized, and provided 'a $20,000 cash payment to each person who was incarcerated.'
c-us6-home-redress.label: consensus

c-us6-home-hawaii.text: In Trump v. Hawaii (2018), in an opinion upholding the president's travel proclamation, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote: 'Korematsu was gravely wrong the day it was decided, has been overruled in the court of history'.
c-us6-home-hawaii.label: consensus

c-us6-home-signs.text: In June 2025 directives of the Interior Department and the National Park Service, issued under the executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History', put up signs at Manzanar and Minidoka inviting visitors to report negative content. The Japanese American National Museum said on 18 June 2025 that it was 'deeply disturbed by this new directive', and on 20 September 2025 The Washington Post reported that a sign about 'the detention of Japanese Americans during World War II' had been removed at at least one additional park. In June 2026 Judge Angel Kelley of the U.S. District Court ordered the administration to restore park signage removed in 2025; KQED reported (15 June 2026) that at Manzanar 'QR codes were posted soliciting public input on what should be taken down'. On 2 July 2026 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit stayed that order, finding, as Bloomberg Law reported, that the Interior Department was likely to succeed in its appeal.
c-us6-home-signs.label: debated
c-us6-home-signs.note: The administration presents the review as restoring 'truth' to the parks' history; the Japanese American National Museum calls it historical erasure. Status as reported in July 2026, with the appeal pending; this book has not confirmed whether any sign at Manzanar or Minidoka was later removed or restored.

c-us6-home-bracero.text: Under the Bracero Program Mexican workers came to the United States on labor contracts: 'From 1942 to 1964, 4.6 million contracts were signed', a count of contracts, not of individual workers.
c-us6-home-bracero.label: consensus

c-us6-home-zoot.text: In the Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles, 3-10 June 1943, 'Many zoot-suiters were beaten by servicemen and stripped of their zoot suits on the spot.'
c-us6-home-zoot.label: consensus

c-us6-war-midway.text: At the Battle of Midway, 4-7 June 1942, 'Against the loss of one U.S. carrier, the Japanese lost four—all of which had participated in the Pearl Harbor attack.' The American carrier lost was Yorktown.
c-us6-war-midway.label: consensus

c-us6-war-dday.text: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, 'nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed by sea and air' in Normandy, on beaches that included Utah and Omaha.
c-us6-war-dday.label: approx

c-us6-war-va.text: The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 16,112,566 Americans who served in the Second World War, with 291,557 battle deaths, 113,842 other deaths in service and 670,846 non-mortal woundings.
c-us6-war-va.label: approx
c-us6-war-va.note: Official VA counts; the National WWII Museum gives slightly different totals.

c-us6-war-museum.text: The National WWII Museum gives 407,316 Americans killed and 671,278 wounded, and 5,662 merchant mariners dead.
c-us6-war-museum.label: approx
c-us6-war-museum.note: The Museum's totals, which differ slightly from the VA's.

c-us6-war-seg.text: The armed forces were segregated through the war; more than one million Black men were inducted, from 2.5 million who registered. 'On July 26, 1948, President Harry S. Truman signed this executive order banning segregation in the Armed Forces.'
c-us6-war-seg.label: approx
c-us6-war-seg.note: The induction and registration figures are the National Archives' round numbers.

c-us6-war-wrb.text: After a Treasury memorandum titled 'The Acquiescence of this Government in the Murder of the Jews', Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9417 on 22 January 1944. It created the War Refugee Board and made it government policy to take 'all measures within its power to rescue the victims of enemy oppression'. (The Treasury's draft had spoken of the 'immediate rescue and relief of the Jews of Europe'.)
c-us6-war-wrb.label: consensus

c-us6-war-wrbsaved.text: The War Refugee Board claimed to have saved 'tens of thousands of lives'.
c-us6-war-wrbsaved.label: approx

c-us6-war-mccloy.text: On 14 August 1944 Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy refused requests to bomb Auschwitz, writing that such an operation 'would in any case be of such doubtful efficacy that it would not warrant the use of our resources'.
c-us6-war-mccloy.label: consensus

c-us6-war-farben.text: The IG Farben industrial complex next to Auschwitz was 'bombed four times in the final year of the war'.
c-us6-war-farben.label: consensus

c-us6-war-wyman.text: David S. Wyman (The Abandonment of the Jews, 1984) argues, as his publisher summarizes the book, that a serious American rescue effort could almost certainly have saved several hundred thousand Jews.
c-us6-war-wyman.label: debated
c-us6-war-wyman.note: Wyman's case for what rescue could have done is disputed by William D. Rubinstein and by studies that judge bombing Auschwitz infeasible; Richard Breitman and Allan Lichtman give a more favourable account of Roosevelt.

c-us6-war-rubinstein.text: William D. Rubinstein (The Myth of Rescue, 1997) argues, as his publisher summarizes the book, that few of the Jews who perished could have been saved by any action of the Allies.
c-us6-war-rubinstein.label: debated

c-us6-war-breitman.text: Richard Breitman and Allan J. Lichtman (FDR and the Jews, 2013) conclude, as American University's news release summarizes them, that Roosevelt did far more to help European Jews than any other world leader of his time.
c-us6-war-breitman.label: debated
c-us6-war-breitman.note: A middle position between Wyman's indictment and Rubinstein's defense; it concerns Roosevelt's record as a whole rather than the bombing question alone.

c-us6-war-bombing.text: Mitchell Bard, in the Jewish Virtual Library, notes that 'Several recent studies have suggested that it was not possible to bomb the camp', citing studies by James Kitchens and Richard Levy, but adds that Stuart Erdheim, in 'perhaps the most exhaustive analysis of the issue', argues that bombing the camp would have been 'no more complex than numerous other missions.'
c-us6-war-bombing.label: debated
c-us6-war-bombing.note: Both sides of the feasibility argument, as summarized by the Jewish Virtual Library; Kitchens's, Levy's and Erdheim's own texts were not checked. Wyman held that the camp could have been bombed.

c-us6-bomb-med.text: 'In August, the Corps set up the Manhattan Engineer District (MED) to manage the project'; Leslie Groves was put in charge in September 1942, and Roosevelt gave his final authorization in December 1942.
c-us6-bomb-med.label: consensus

c-us6-bomb-sites.text: The project's main sites were Oak Ridge in Tennessee, Hanford in Washington and Los Alamos in New Mexico. 'At its peak, the project employed 130,000 workers', and it cost about $2.2 billion. The first bomb was exploded in the 'Trinity Test on July 16, 1945'.
c-us6-bomb-sites.label: approx
c-us6-bomb-sites.note: The worker and cost figures are the Department of Energy's round numbers.

c-us6-bomb-fdr.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt 'died April 12, 1945, Warm Springs, Georgia'.
c-us6-bomb-fdr.label: consensus

c-us6-bomb-truman.text: On 6 August 1945 President Truman announced: 'Sixteen hours ago an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima, an important Japanese Army base.' And: 'It is an atomic bomb.'
c-us6-bomb-truman.label: consensus

c-us6-bomb-nagasaki.text: A second atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945.
c-us6-bomb-nagasaki.label: consensus

c-us6-bomb-rerf.text: The Radiation Effects Research Foundation estimates that within two to four months the bombs killed 90,000 to 166,000 people in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki, and says the total is 'not known precisely'.
c-us6-bomb-rerf.label: approx
c-us6-bomb-rerf.note: A range, because the records of 1945 are incomplete.

c-us6-bomb-ussbs.text: The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey (1946) put the dead at 'between 70,000 and 80,000' in Hiroshima and 'over 35,000 dead' in Nagasaki.
c-us6-bomb-ussbs.label: approx
c-us6-bomb-ussbs.note: An early American estimate, lower than the later RERF range.

c-us6-bomb-city.text: The City of Hiroshima estimates that '237,000 people were killed directly or indirectly' by the Hiroshima bomb.
c-us6-bomb-city.label: approx
c-us6-bomb-city.note: A long-term count that includes indirect deaths, as reported by the Atomic Heritage Foundation.

c-us6-bomb-alperovitz.text: Gar Alperovitz, writing in The Nation in 2015, argues that American military leaders and intelligence judged Japan to be on the verge of surrender, and that the Japanese moved to surrender only after the Soviet Union entered the war; 'By and large, the top generals and admirals who managed World War II knew better.'
c-us6-bomb-alperovitz.label: debated
c-us6-bomb-alperovitz.note: The revisionist view. Robert P. Newman and Richard B. Frank defend the decision; Tsuyoshi Hasegawa also stresses Soviet entry.

c-us6-bomb-newman.text: Robert P. Newman (Truman and the Hiroshima Cult, 1995) holds, as the book's description summarizes it, that Truman used the bomb to end the war as quickly and with as few casualties as possible.
c-us6-bomb-newman.label: debated
c-us6-bomb-newman.note: Against Alperovitz's view that the bomb was not needed to end the war.

c-us6-bomb-frank.text: Richard B. Frank, the author of Downfall, wrote in an H-Diplo roundtable on Tsuyoshi Hasegawa's Racing the Enemy: 'I believe that anyone who could conceivably have been president in 1945 would have authorized the use of the atomic bombs', given the radio intelligence on Japan's preparations to meet the planned invasion.
c-us6-bomb-frank.label: debated
c-us6-bomb-frank.note: Frank defends the decision; Alperovitz and Hasegawa stress Soviet entry into the war.

c-us6-bomb-hasegawa.text: Tsuyoshi Hasegawa (Racing the Enemy, 2005) writes, in a passage Frank quotes in the roundtable: 'The evidence is compelling that Soviet entry into the war had a strong impact on the peace party. Indeed, the Soviet attack, not the Hiroshima bomb, convinced political leaders to end the war by accepting the Potsdam Proclamation.'
c-us6-bomb-hasegawa.label: debated
c-us6-bomb-hasegawa.note: Hasegawa's words as Frank quotes them (pp. 198-99); Frank's commentary disputes how much Soviet entry, against the bombs, weighed in Japan's surrender.

c-us6-bomb-un.text: At the San Francisco conference, 25 April to 26 June 1945, 'Representatives of 50 countries gathered'. The Charter of the United Nations 'was signed on 26 June 1945, in San Francisco', and came into force on 24 October 1945.
c-us6-bomb-un.label: consensus

pages.title: Depression, New Deal and war
pages.lede: Real output fell by about a quarter between 1929 and 1933, when unemployment reached 24.9 percent in the series Stanley Lebergott published in 1957, which for 1929-39 uses the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates of 1948. By 1944 output was more than twice its 1929 level and unemployment was 1.2 percent, while federal outlays had risen from about 3 percent of GDP in 1929 to about 41 percent.
body: The 1920s began with a slump. A 'sharp deflation in 1920' lasted 'about one year', [[c-us6-20s-harding]] and on Stanley Lebergott's estimates unemployment was 11.9 percent in 1921 but only 1.9 percent in 1926. [[c-us6-ov-unemp]] The Bureau of Economic Analysis's GDP series begins only in 1929. For earlier years MeasuringWorth's reconstruction puts real GDP at $822.1 billion in 1921 and $1,127.1 billion in 1928, in 2017 dollars, a rise of about 37 percent. Because it is a different series, it is not strictly comparable with BEA's figures from 1929 on, and the chart on this page does not join the two. [[c-us6-ov-mw]]

In BEA's series real GDP fell from $1,191.1 billion in 1929 to $877.4 billion in 1933, about 26 percent, in chained 2017 dollars. [[c-us6-ov-gdp]] Unemployment rose from 3.2 percent in 1929 to 24.9 percent in 1933. [[c-us6-ov-unemp]] These figures are reconstructions: in 1948 the Monthly Labor Review explained that 'Estimates for the period 1929-39 were prepared by the Bureau of Labor Statistics', which put the number unemployed in 1933 at 12,830,000. [[c-us6-ov-bls]] Output was back above its 1929 level in 1936, yet unemployment was still 17.0 percent that year, and it rose again from 14.3 percent in 1937 to 19.0 percent in 1938. [[c-us6-ov-gdp]] [[c-us6-ov-unemp]] On the Depression worldwide, see 15.4; on its causes, US6.5.

War transformed the figures. Federal net outlays, $3,127 million in fiscal 1929 and $9,468 million in 1940, reached $92,712 million in 1945. [[c-us6-ov-outlays]] As a share of GDP they were about 3.0 percent in 1929, 9.8 percent in 1934 and 40.7 percent in 1944; the series divides fiscal-year outlays by calendar-year GDP. [[c-us6-ov-share]] Real GDP peaked in 1944 at $2,524.8 billion, more than twice its 1929 level, [[c-us6-ov-gdp]] and unemployment fell to 1.2 percent. [[c-us6-ov-unemp]] On the Second World War in global terms, see 15.6.

This chapter takes the 1920s first: the economy (US6.1), the culture wars (US6.2), immigration restriction (US6.3) and Black America (US6.4). It then turns to the Crash and the Depression (US6.5), the New Deal and the debates over it (US6.6-US6.8), the Dust Bowl and the politics of faith (US6.9), and the road to war, the home front and the war itself (US6.10-US6.13). On the First World War at home and the Red Scare, see US5.13; on the Commerce Clause, US2.2.

practice.q: Why does this page's GDP chart begin in 1929 rather than 1920?
choices: BEA's series starts in 1929; the 1920s figures come from another series
Real GDP barely changed in the 1920s, so those years add little
No unemployment estimates exist for the years before the 1929 crash
The figures for the 1920s are in current dollars, not adjusted for prices
practice.why: The Bureau of Economic Analysis's series starts in 1929. MeasuringWorth's academic reconstruction covers the 1920s, but it is a different series and not strictly comparable.

wrong.1: MeasuringWorth's figures rise from $822.1 billion in 1921 to $1,127.1 billion in 1928, about 37 percent.
wrong.2: Lebergott's series gives 11.9 percent for 1921 and 1.9 percent for 1926.
wrong.3: MeasuringWorth's figures are real GDP in 2017 dollars.

practice.q: Federal outlays were about 3 percent of GDP in 1929, about 10 percent in 1934 and about 41 percent in 1944. What does this chiefly show?
choices: War spending, far more than the New Deal, made federal outlays a large share
Federal outlays fell in dollars from 1929 to 1939, then rose for the war
The New Deal had already pushed outlays above 30 percent of GDP by 1934
The New Deal and the war raised the share by about the same amount
practice.why: The share was about 3.0 percent in 1929, 9.8 percent in 1934 and 40.7 percent in 1944: the large jump came with the war.

wrong.2: The share in 1934 was about 9.8 percent.
wrong.3: The share rose by under 7 points from 1929 to 1934, and by about 31 points from 1934 to 1944.

pages.title: The 1920s economy
pages.lede: Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts between 1908 and 1927 as the price fell from $850 to as little as $260, and by 1932 two-thirds of American dwellings had electricity, though only 11 percent of farm dwellings did. Households bought most durables on instalments while farm prices collapsed, the top income-tax rate fell from 73 to 25 percent, and the Dow closed at its peak of 381.17 on 3 September 1929.
body: 'From 1908-1927, Ford Motor Company produced over 15 million Model T cars', and 'the price dropped from $850 to as little as $260.' [[c-us6-20s-ford]] Ford began building magnetos on 'a crude moving assembly line in April 1913' at Highland Park. The moving line turned out 'a finished Model T every 93 minutes', against 12½ hours per car under stationary assembly. [[c-us6-20s-line]]

Electricity reached most homes in these years. 'In 1907, only 8 percent of all dwellings were using electricity; by 1932, this figure had risen to 67 percent.' But by 1932 more than 80 percent of urban dwellings had service, against only 11 percent of farm dwellings. [[c-us6-20s-elec]] KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the Harding-Cox election returns on 2 November 1920, and within four years 600 stations existed in the United States. [[c-us6-20s-radio]] Martha Olney's notes put 70 to 90 percent of consumer durables in the 1920s as bought on instalments, and the ratio of consumer debt to income doubled. [[c-us6-20s-credit]] Olney argues that this debt mattered when the economy turned down: households cut other spending to avoid default, and 'Consumer spending collapsed in 1930, turning a minor recession into the Great Depression.' Hers is one explanation among several (US6.5). [[c-us6-20s-olney]]

Farm prices fell. 'From 1919 to 1920, corn tumbled from $1.30 per bushel to forty-seven cents' in Minnesota, by MNopedia's figures. [[c-us6-20s-farm]] Harding took office during a 'sharp deflation in 1920, which lasted for about one year', and signed the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921, which 'allowed the President to present a unified budget for the first time.' [[c-us6-20s-harding]] Congress twice passed the McNary-Haugen farm relief bill, and Coolidge vetoed it both times. [[c-us6-20s-coolidge]]

Under Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon the top income-tax rate fell from 73 percent to 58 percent under the Revenue Act of 1921, then to 46 percent in 1924 and 25 percent in 1926. [[c-us6-20s-mellon]] Christopher Frenze's 1982 staff study for the Joint Economic Committee argues that the cuts raised revenue from the rich: between 1921 and 1922, after the first cut, income taxes paid by those reporting incomes of $50,000 or more rose from $318 million to $446 million. The Miller Center's essay on Coolidge says the cuts favoured the rich and that Coolidge's policies 'contributed to the stock market crash of 1929'. Gene Smiley and Richard Keehn (1995) argue that a primary motive for the cuts was to reduce tax avoidance by wealthier people, and that the cuts did reduce it. [[c-us6-20s-mellondebate]] The Dow Jones average rose from 63 in August 1921 until 'the index peaked on September 3, 1929, closing at 381.17'. Buyers on margin put down 'typically 10 percent, and borrowed the rest.' [[c-us6-20s-dow]] The crash itself is the subject of US6.5.

pages.title: The culture wars of the 1920s
pages.lede: The Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture, sale and transport of intoxicating liquors for drinking; one study estimates that consumption fell to about 30 percent of its earlier level and recovered to 60-70 percent, and the Twenty-first Amendment ended Prohibition in December 1933. In 1925 a Tennessee jury convicted Scopes under a law against teaching any theory that denied the Bible's account of creation, while estimates of the Klan's peak membership run from about one million to several million.
body: The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified on 16 January 1919, prohibited 'the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors … for beverage purposes', to take effect 'After one year from the ratification of this article'. [[c-us6-cult-18th]] The Volstead Act of October 1919 enforced it and defined intoxicating liquor as anything above 0.5 percent alcohol; Congress passed it over President Wilson's veto. [[c-us6-cult-volstead]] Did people stop drinking? Jeffrey Miron and Jeffrey Zwiebel estimate, from mortality, mental-health and crime statistics, that consumption 'fell sharply at the beginning of Prohibition, to approximately 30 percent' of its earlier level, then recovered 'to about 60-70 percent of its pre-prohibition level'. [[c-us6-cult-miron]]

In the ABA Journal's account, 'The rise of organized crime syndicates, spurred by a flourishing bootlegging industry' fed the movement for repeal. [[c-us6-cult-crime]] The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth, ratified through conventions in the states; on 5 December 1933 Utah became the 36th state to approve it. [[c-us6-cult-21st]]

In his sermon of 21 May 1922, 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' (printed in The Christian Work on 10 June), Harry Emerson Fosdick attacked the demand that believers accept the virgin birth and a Bible God had 'inerrantly dictated to men a good deal as a man might dictate to a stenographer.' [[c-us6-cult-fosdick]] Tennessee's Butler Act made it unlawful 'to teach any theory that denies the story of divine creation as taught by the Bible'. Scopes's trial opened in Dayton on 10 July 1925, and on 21 July the jury found him guilty after 10 minutes. [[c-us6-cult-scopes]] Clarence Darrow questioned William Jennings Bryan about Jonah and the whale and about Joshua making the sun stand still; [[c-us6-cult-bryan]] the verse reads, in the NRSVUE, 'And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance on their enemies.' [[c-us6-cult-joshua]] Bryan died days after the trial. [[c-us6-cult-bryan]] On appeal, in January 1927, the Tennessee Supreme Court upheld the law but set aside the conviction because of the way the fine had been set. [[c-us6-cult-appeal]]

How big was the second Ku Klux Klan? 'At its peak, the Klan claimed to have four to six million members or more', Scott McLemee notes. Linda Gordon, the author of The Second Coming of the KKK, told TIME in 2017 that 'At its peak, the Klan numbered between 3 million and 5 million people in the North'. McLemee argues that the claim is credible only if it includes four or five million who signed up and soon quit, which 'would leave a million members'. [[c-us6-cult-klan]] In Indiana, the publisher's description of Leonard Moore's Citizen Klansmen says more than 25 percent of native-born men joined; the History Museum in South Bend gives 250,000 white men, about 30 percent of the state's native-born white men. Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson was convicted of second-degree murder in the death of Madge Oberholtzer. [[c-us6-cult-indiana]] On the Klan of Reconstruction, see US4.11.

pages.title: Closing the gates
pages.lede: Quota laws in 1921 and 1924 cut the annual cap on quota immigration from about 350,000 to 164,667, set by nationality, and the 1924 act excluded immigrants from Asia. In the 1930s Mexicans and Americans of Mexican descent were repatriated to Mexico in numbers that scholars estimate at about 400,000 to one million, and that California's legislature, in a statute of 2005, put at two million.
body: 'On May 19, 1921, President Warren Harding signed the Quota Act of 1921.' It admitted each year 3 percent of the foreign-born of each nationality counted in the 1910 census, about 350,000 people, and it 'did not, however, establish quotas of any kind for residents of the Western Hemisphere'. [[c-us6-imm-1921]] On the literacy test of 1917 and the immigration that came before, see US5.4.

The Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 cut the quota to 2 percent and 'pushed back the year on which quota calculations were based from 1910 to 1890'. It 'capped quota immigration at 164,667 people per year', and under the national-origins system, from 1929, the cap was 153,879. [[c-us6-imm-1924]] By barring aliens ineligible for citizenship, the act 'completely excluded immigrants from Asia'. 'The Japanese government protested, but the law remained.' [[c-us6-imm-asia]]

Sacco and Vanzetti were tried in 1921 for a payroll robbery and murder and executed on 23 August 1927. In 1977 Governor Michael Dukakis of Massachusetts proclaimed that 'any stigma and disgrace' should be removed from their names, declaring that 'The atmosphere of their trial and appeals was permeated by prejudice against foreigners'. [[c-us6-imm-sacco]] Whether they were guilty is a separate question and still disputed: Douglas Linder's account reports that a ballistics test in 1961 gave 'strong evidence that Sacco did indeed fire a fatal bullet', and that some argue one man may have been guilty and the other innocent. [[c-us6-imm-saccoguilt]]

How many people of Mexican descent were sent or went to Mexico in the 1930s? As summarised by Lee, Peri and Yasenov, Hoffman (1974) put the number at 400,000 to 500,000, Gratton and Merchant (2013), with Hoffman, at about 400,000, and Balderrama and Rodríguez (2006) at up to one million. Lee, Peri and Yasenov (2022), who write that the lower figures fit the census data better, describe an episode in which 'at least 400,000 Mexicans returned to Mexico between 1929 and 1934'. [[c-us6-imm-repat]] California's legislature, in a statute of 2005, states that 'it is estimated that two million people of Mexican ancestry were forcibly relocated', 'approximately 1.2 million of whom had been born in the United States'; that is the legislature's figure, not a scholarly estimate. [[c-us6-imm-calif]] Did their departure help native workers? Lee, Peri and Yasenov find that it did not: 'Mexican repatriations resulted in reduced employment and occupational downgrading for U.S. natives.' [[c-us6-imm-lpylabor]]

pages.title: Black America
pages.lede: About 2 million Black people left the South from the First World War to the Second. In Tulsa in 1921 a mob destroyed 35 blocks of Greenwood; Oklahoma's commission judged in 2001 that the dead likely numbered between 100 and 300, and a federal review of January 2025 called it 'a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood'. In the Scottsboro case the Supreme Court held in 1932 and 1935 that the Fourteenth Amendment required effective counsel in capital cases and barred the exclusion of Black citizens from juries.
body: According to the National Archives, 'From World War I until World War II, it is estimated that about 2 million Black people left the South', and the Census Bureau estimates 6 million between 1910 and 1970. [[c-us6-black-migration]] The Metropolitan Museum of Art treats the Harlem Renaissance as part of 'the new Black cities that took shape in the 1920s–40s'; its artists included Aaron Douglas, Augusta Savage and James Van Der Zee. [[c-us6-black-harlem]] Marcus Garvey co-founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914 and arrived in Harlem in 1916. His trial for mail fraud began on 18 May 1923, and on 21 June he was sentenced to five years in prison; his sentence was commuted, and in 1927 he was deported, 'never to return'. He died in London in 1940, and President Biden pardoned him posthumously on 19 January 2025. [[c-us6-black-garvey]]

On 31 May and 1 June 1921 a mob destroyed 35 blocks of Tulsa's Greenwood district and about 1,256 homes. [[c-us6-black-tulsa]] How many died is uncertain. Oklahoma's commission, reporting on 28 February 2001, judged that the dead likely numbered between 100 and 300, and reported that its forensic anthropologist, Clyde Snow, could identify 38 victims 'By the most conservative of all possible methods'. [[c-us6-black-toll]] The Justice Department's review, announced on 10 January 2025, called the massacre 'a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood' in which some police took part in 'murder, arson and looting', but found 'no living perpetrator' who could be prosecuted. [[c-us6-black-doj]]

The survivors went to court. In June 2024 the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed their suit, brought under Oklahoma's public nuisance law; as Lessie Benningfield Randle's lawyer said on 30 May 2026, 'Unfortunately our litigation was ended back in 2024'. [[c-us6-black-court]] Viola Fletcher died at 111, as KGOU reported on 24 November 2025. As of 6 October 2026, Lessie Benningfield Randle was alive at 111. [[c-us6-black-survivors]] On 1 June 2025 Tulsa's mayor, Monroe Nichols, announced a plan, the Road to Repair, under which a Greenwood Trust would be created with the goal of securing $105 million in assets, most of it secured or committed by 1 June 2026. This book has not confirmed how much had been raised by that date. [[c-us6-black-trust]]

On 25 March 1931 nine Black youths, aged 13 to 19 by Prologue's account, were seized at Paint Rock, Alabama, and first tried at Scottsboro, the Jackson County seat, in April 1931. The International Labor Defense, 'the legal arm of the Communist Party', ran their defence, and one accuser, Ruby Bates, recanted and testified for the defence at Haywood Patterson's second trial in 1933 that there had been no rape. [[c-us6-black-scottsboro]] In Powell v. Alabama (1932) the Supreme Court held that the failure to provide effective counsel in a capital case was 'a denial of due process within the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment'; in Norris v. Alabama (1935) it held that evidence that no Black citizen had been called for jury service 'for a generation or longer' 'established the discrimination which the Constitution forbids', a denial of equal protection. [[c-us6-black-powell]] On 21 November 2013 Alabama posthumously pardoned Charles Weems, Andy Wright and Haywood Patterson. [[c-us6-black-pardon]] On the Fourteenth Amendment, see US2.11.
