pages.title: The Crash and the Great Depression
pages.lede: A recession had already begun when the stock market crashed in October 1929; by the summer of 1932 the Dow stood 89 percent below its peak. Real output fell by about a quarter to 30 percent, depending on the measure, and about 9,000 banks failed. Economists still weigh the Federal Reserve, spending, the gold standard and the collapse of credit as causes.
body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at 381.17 on 3 September 1929. On Black Monday, 28 October, it fell nearly 13 percent, and the next day nearly 12 percent more; it bottomed at 41.22 in the summer of 1932, 89 percent below its peak, and did not regain its 1929 high until November 1954. [[c-us6-crash-dow]] The crash did not start the downturn: a recession had begun in the summer of 1929. Christina Romer argues that the crash deepened it by cutting purchases of durable goods: 'The stock market crash is the prime source for the collapse in durable goods purchases starting in November 1929.' [[c-us6-crash-romer]] For the Depression outside the United States, see 15.4.

In the Bureau of Economic Analysis series, real GDP fell from $1,191 billion in 1929 to $877 billion in 1933 (in chained 2017 dollars), about 26 percent between the annual averages; Britannica, measuring from the peak to the trough of the downturn, gives 30 percent. [[c-us6-crash-gdp]] Britannica puts the fall in industrial production at 47 percent, and Romer finds that producer prices fell by slightly over 40 percent from July 1929 to July 1932. [[c-us6-crash-ip]] In the standard series of Lebergott and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which for 1929-39 are the same, unemployment peaked in 1933 at 24.9 percent, about a quarter of the labor force; how to count the jobless from 1933 on is disputed (US6.7). [[c-us6-crash-unemp]] [[c-us6-ov-unemp]]

The banks failed in waves: the Caldwell banks of Nashville in November 1930; on 11 December the Bank of United States, the fourth-largest bank in New York City; and banks in Chicago in June 1931 (map, US6.6). [[c-us6-crash-panics]] From the fall of 1930 to the winter of 1933 the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent. [[c-us6-crash-money]] The FDIC counts about 9,000 bank suspensions, with losses to depositors of about $1.3 billion; the Social Security Administration says the failed banks took 'with them $7 billion in depositors' assets'. The figures measure different things: the first is what depositors lost, the second the deposits held in banks that failed. [[c-us6-crash-banks]]

Why was the slump so deep? Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Federal Reserve, which, as their publisher summarises the argument, failed to manage the monetary system and to counter the banking panics. [[c-us6-crash-fs]] Peter Temin (1976) answered, as Kirkus Reviews reported, that 'there is no evidence that the banking panic of 1930 had a deflationary effect on the economy' and that the data were consistent with the spending hypothesis, the view that a fall in spending caused the slump. [[c-us6-crash-temin]] Barry Eichengreen and Temin point to 'the mentality of the gold standard', and Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs found that 'currency depreciation was beneficial for the initiating countries.' [[c-us6-crash-gold]] Ben Bernanke (1983) argued that 'the financial disruptions of 1930-33 reduced the efficiency of the credit allocation process'; the Nobel committee cited this work in 2022. [[c-us6-crash-bernanke]] Historians also debate whether the Tariff Act of 1930 (Smoot-Hawley) provoked foreign retaliation that deepened the Depression. [[c-us6-crash-tariff]]

pages.title: Hoover and the first New Deal
pages.lede: In January 1932 Hoover signed the act creating the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which lent to banks and other financial institutions, insurance companies and railroads. Roosevelt's first months in office, from 4 March 1933, brought a bank holiday, the law creating deposit insurance, the suspension of the gold standard, the AAA, the NIRA and the Civilian Conservation Corps.
body: Banking panics had struck Nashville and New York in 1930 and Chicago in 1931 (US6.5). [[c-us6-crash-panics]] On 22 January 1932 President Hoover signed the Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act. With $500 million in capital, the RFC lent to banks and other financial institutions, insurance companies and railroads, and from July 1932 to states and cities. [[c-us6-nd1-rfc]]

Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated on 4 March 1933. In the American Presidency Project's transcript of the speech as delivered, he said: 'So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.' He declared that 'the money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization', that 'Our greatest primary task is to put people to work', and asked for 'broad Executive power to wage a war against the emergency'. [[c-us6-nd1-inaug]] Two days later Proclamation 2039 closed the banks. Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act on 9 March, banks began to reopen on 13 March, and by 15 March banks holding 90 percent of the system's resources were open again; 'some 4,000 banks would remain closed forever.' [[c-us6-nd1-holiday]]

The Banking Act of 1933, known as Glass-Steagall and signed on 16 June, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and 'effectively separated commercial banking from investment banking'; its limits on affiliations between the two were repealed by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999. [[c-us6-nd1-gs]] On 20 April 1933 the gold standard was suspended, and in June gold clauses in contracts were abrogated. Under the Gold Reserve Act of 30 January 1934, Roosevelt fixed gold at $35 an ounce by proclamation the next day, up from $20.67. 'Scholars believe', in the words of Federal Reserve History, 'Roosevelt's reflation accelerated America's recovery from the Great Depression.' [[c-us6-nd1-gold]] On the Federal Reserve and the money power, see US2.13.

The Agricultural Adjustment Act of May 1933 paid farmers to grow less, aiming to restore farm purchasing power to its level of 1909-14; the Supreme Court struck it down in 1936. [[c-us6-nd1-aaa]] The National Industrial Recovery Act of 16 June set up industry codes of fair competition and funded public works. Its Section 7(a) declared that 'employees shall have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing'. Minorities were enrolled 'at far lower rates than the legislation allowed'. [[c-us6-nd1-ccc]]

pages.title: The second New Deal and the Court
pages.lede: From 1935 the WPA put some 8.5 million people to work, the Social Security Act left about half of workers outside it, and the Wagner Act protected the right to join unions. The Supreme Court struck down the NIRA's code system in 1935; Roosevelt's plan to enlarge the Court failed in 1937, but that spring the Court upheld a minimum-wage law.
body: The Works Progress Administration, created in 1935, put some 8.5 million people to work at a cost of about $11 billion before it ended in 1943. [[c-us6-nd2-wpa]] Whether such relief workers count as employed changes the record of the decade. Lebergott and the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted them as unemployed; Michael Darby, in an NBER working paper of 1975, called this 'A major conceptual error', and in that paper counting them as employed brings unemployment in 1936 down from 17.0 to 10.1 percent. [[c-us6-crash-unemp]] The two series are identical until 1932 and diverge from 1933 (chart); in the version Darby published in 1976, as Robert Margo tabulates it, the rate for 1936 is 9.9 percent. [[c-us6-crash-series]]

The Social Security Act of 1935, writes Larry DeWitt of the Social Security Administration, 'excluded from coverage about half the workers in the American economy', among them agricultural and domestic workers; 65 percent of African American workers fell outside it, and '27 percent of the white workforce was likewise excluded from coverage.' [[c-us6-nd2-excl]] Why is debated. Ira Katznelson stresses the power of southern members of Congress, and, as a Columbia Magazine review summarises his argument, holds that the New Deal in effect traded away Black Americans' interests to win major benefits for whites; Robert Lieberman and Linda Gordon also see a racial motive. [[c-us6-nd2-katz]] DeWitt, answering Lieberman, Gordon and others, concludes that 'the racial-bias thesis is both conceptually flawed and unsupported', and that the exclusion 'was due to considerations of administrative feasibility involving tax-collection procedures.' [[c-us6-nd2-dewitt]]

The Wagner Act of 5 July 1935 gave employees the right to form and join unions, required employers to bargain with unions chosen by a majority, and created the National Labor Relations Board. [[c-us6-nd2-wagner]] The Fair Labor Standards Act, signed on 25 June 1938, set a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and a 44-hour week at first, and banned oppressive child labor; it covered industries employing only about one-fifth of the labor force. [[c-us6-nd2-flsa]]

On 27 May 1935 a unanimous Supreme Court ruled against the NIRA's code system in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States: 'Extraordinary conditions do not create or enlarge constitutional power'. [[c-us6-nd2-schechter]] For the commerce power and judicial review, see US2.2 and US2.6. On 5 February 1937 Roosevelt proposed to add a justice for each sitting justice over 70, up to six. The Senate Judiciary Committee called it 'an invasion of judicial power such as has never before been attempted in this country', and the plan was shelved by July. [[c-us6-nd2-court]] Meanwhile, on 29 March 1937, the Court upheld a minimum-wage law by 5 to 4 in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, overruling Adkins (1923): 'The Constitution does not speak of freedom of contract.' [[c-us6-nd2-wch]] Whether Justice Owen Roberts changed his vote because of the plan is debated. The legal historian G. Edward White notes that the justices had first voted on the case at their conference of 19 December 1936, where Roberts voted to sustain the Washington law, before the plan was introduced in February 1937. The 'switch in time' reading, which William Leuchtenburg describes as the view of contemporaries, ties the decision to the plan; White concludes that Roberts's switch 'had nothing to do with the introduction of the Court-packing plan'. [[c-us6-nd2-switch]]

pages.title: Did the New Deal work?
pages.lede: Real GDP grew about 43 percent from 1933 to 1937 and passed its 1929 level in 1936, before the recession of 1937-38. Economists disagree over what drove the recovery and what held it back: Romer credits gold inflows and money, Cole and Ohanian blame cartelization, Eggertsson disputes them, and Fishback has measured the programmes one by one. The effects of the HOLC's redlining maps are also disputed.
body: In the BEA series real GDP rose from $877 billion in 1933 to $1,257 billion in 1937 (chained 2017 dollars), about 43 percent, passing its 1929 level in 1936; Britannica gives growth of 9 percent a year from 1933 to 1937. [[c-us6-eval-gdp]] Then a recession ran from May 1937 to June 1938: real GDP fell 10 percent from peak to trough and unemployment rose back to 20 percent. Federal Reserve History notes that 'Fed policymakers doubled reserve requirement ratios', and also lists the Treasury's sterilization of gold, the new Social Security payroll tax and tighter fiscal policy. [[c-us6-eval-1937]] On how unemployment is counted, see US6.7. [[c-us6-crash-unemp]]

What drove the recovery? Christina Romer argues that 'nearly all of the observed recovery of the U.S. economy prior to 1942 was due to monetary expansion', fed by 'Huge gold inflows'. [[c-us6-eval-romer]] Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian (2004) conclude that 'New Deal cartelization policies are an important factor in accounting for the failure of the economy to recover back to trend.' [[c-us6-eval-co]] Gauti Eggertsson (2012) replies that with zero interest rates and falling prices, conditions he finds 'satisfied during the Great Depression', such policies were expansionary in his model. [[c-us6-eval-egg]]

Price Fishback has measured the programmes one by one. With Valentina Kachanovskaya he finds that a federal dollar raised state income per person 'by between 40 and 96 cents', with 'no positive effects on private employment.' [[c-us6-eval-fk]] In his survey, relief and public works had income multipliers 'of around one' and 'reduced crime rates, and lowered several types of mortality'; the farm programs 'typically aided large farm owners but eliminated opportunities for share croppers, tenants, and farm workers'; and the Home Owners' Loan Corporation 'staved off drops in housing prices and home ownership rates'. [[c-us6-eval-survey]]

The HOLC's maps of the 1930s, which marked some neighborhoods in red, are disputed. Daniel Aaronson, Daniel Hartley and Bhashkar Mazumder (2021) find that 'The maps led to reduced home ownership rates, house values, and rents' and 'increased racial segregation in later decades.' [[c-us6-eval-ahm]] Fishback, Jonathan Rose, Kenneth Snowden and Thomas Storrs (2021; 2024) argue that the Federal Housing Administration redlined first, that 'the HOLC itself broadly loaned to such neighborhoods and to Black homeowners', and that 'the HOLC's redlining maps had little effect on the geographic distribution of either program's mortgage market activity'. In a Chicago Fed brief (2022), Rose, one of the co-authors, concluded that the FHA's red lines were 'likely far more impactful than the HOLC's.' [[c-us6-eval-frss]]

pages.title: Dust, demagogues and faith
pages.lede: Drought and the plowing of marginal land produced the Dust Bowl, and 300,000 to 400,000 people from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and Missouri settled in California, few of them from the Dust Bowl itself. Huey Long proposed to cap fortunes, and the priest and broadcaster Charles Coughlin turned to antisemitism. Pius XI taught a family wage and subsidiarity, while the Catholic Worker and Black churches offered hospitality and food to the poor.
body: Strictly, the Dust Bowl covered western Kansas, southeastern Colorado and the Oklahoma Panhandle, with adjoining areas. Droughts struck in 1930-31, 1934, 1936 and 1939-40. Low crop prices, pushed lower by a record wheat crop in 1931, and high machinery costs led farmers to put more submarginal land into production, while the one-way disc plow 'greatly increased the risk of blowing soil'. [[c-us6-faith-dust]] On Black Sunday, 14 April 1935, a dust storm hit Boise City, Oklahoma, at about 5:15 pm; the name 'Dust Bowl' is generally traced to an Associated Press report about it published the next day. [[c-us6-faith-black]] James Gregory estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 people from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and Missouri settled in California in the 1930s, but 'The actual Dust Bowl counties were sparsely populated and contributed few refugees.' [[c-us6-faith-okies]]

Huey Long's Share Our Wealth plan, set out in the Congressional Record in 1934-35, would have limited fortunes to 'not more than $3 to 4 million', let every family 'possess not less than $5,000 free of debt' and an income 'of not less than $2,500 per year', and paid 'Old-age pensions of $30 per month to persons over 60 years of age'. [[c-us6-faith-long]] Charles Coughlin, a priest at the Shrine of the Little Flower in Royal Oak, Michigan, reached a regular radio audience that the US Holocaust Memorial Museum puts at 30 million. In 1933 he hailed the New Deal as Christ's Deal, while, by the museum's account, already attacking bankers as 'modern Shylocks', a phrase that drew on antisemitic stereotypes. Ten days after Kristallnacht, in November 1938, he claimed that Jews controlled the radio and the press, and that year his magazine Social Justice serialized the antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. His archbishop ordered him to stop broadcasting in 1941, and on 1 May 1942 told him to stop all non-pastoral activities or risk being defrocked. [[c-us6-faith-coughlin]] On the Holocaust, see 15.7.

In Quadragesimo Anno (15 May 1931) Pope Pius XI taught that 'the worker must be paid a wage sufficient to support him and his family', and stated the principle of subsidiarity: 'Just as it is gravely wrong to take from individuals what they can accomplish by their own initiative and industry and give it to the community, so also it is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.' He also declared that 'no one can be at the same time a good Catholic and a true socialist'. [[c-us6-faith-qa]] Compare Rerum Novarum (US5.9). The Catholic Worker, founded in New York City in 1933 by Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin, ran houses of hospitality that welcomed the poor as guests rather than as clients. [[c-us6-faith-cw]]

In Chicago, the historian Wallace Best finds, Black migrants flocked to storefront churches. Elder Lucy Smith's church fed as many as about 90 people a day, and Best found no mainline Black church giving such relief. [[c-us6-faith-best]] Father Divine's Peace Mission Movement served food at very low prices and was racially integrated. [[c-us6-faith-divine]] On the Great Migration, see US6.4.

pages.title: From neutrality to war
pages.lede: From 1935 Congress passed Neutrality Acts that banned arms exports and loans to nations at war, and in 1939 it let belligerents buy arms for cash and carry them away. In 1939 the United States refused the refugees of the St. Louis and let a bill to admit 20,000 refugee children die in committee, while about 118,000 German quota places went unused between 1933 and 1941. Lend-Lease and the Atlantic Charter followed in 1941, and on 8 December Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war on Japan.
body: 'On August 31, 1935, Congress passed the first Neutrality Act', which banned the export of arms to nations at war. A law of 1936 added a ban on loans to belligerents, and one of 1937 let the president allow them to buy goods other than arms on a 'cash-and-carry' basis. [[c-us6-neut-acts]] The Neutrality Act of November 1939 lifted the arms embargo and put all trade with belligerents on cash-and-carry terms. American ships were barred from belligerent ports, and 'The ban on loans remained in effect.' [[c-us6-neut-1939]] Outside Congress, the America First Committee opposed entry into the war and claimed 800,000 members. [[c-us6-neut-afc]] At its rally in Des Moines on 11 September 1941, Charles Lindbergh accused Great Britain, Jews and the Roosevelt administration of leading the United States into war. [[c-us6-neut-lindbergh]]

(On the quota laws, see US6.3; on the Holocaust, 15.7.) The St. Louis left Hamburg on 13 May 1939 with 937 passengers. Cuba, the United States and Canada all refused them, and in the end 254 of the passengers were killed in the Holocaust. [[c-us6-neut-stlouis]] The Wagner-Rogers bill, introduced on 9 February 1939, would have admitted 20,000 refugee children aged 14 and under over two years. It died in the Senate Immigration Committee in the first week of July. [[c-us6-neut-wagner]] The quotas were treated as ceilings. The German quota was 25,957 a year, yet between 1933 and 1941, by the Holocaust Museum's estimate, roughly 118,000 German places that could have been used went unfilled. From July 1941 visa control was centralized in Washington. [[c-us6-neut-quotas]]

Lend-Lease, 'An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States', was approved on 11 March 1941, and the program eventually dispensed some $50 billion in assistance. [[c-us6-neut-lendlease]] On 9-10 August Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard USS Augusta in Placentia Bay, and on 14 August they released a joint declaration of eight principles, the Atlantic Charter. Its first principle reads: 'First, their countries seek no aggrandizement, territorial or other'. Its third reads: 'Third, they respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live'. [[c-us6-neut-atlantic]]

On 8 December 1941 Roosevelt went before a joint session of Congress: 'Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.' He closed: 'I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.' [[c-us6-neut-infamy]] His draft had read 'a date which will live in world history'. [[c-us6-neut-draft]] The America First Committee dissolved after Pearl Harbor. [[c-us6-neut-afc]] For the war in Europe and Asia as a whole, see 15.6.

pages.title: The home front
pages.lede: Real GDP rose by about 92 percent between 1939 and 1944, federal outlays climbed from under a tenth of GDP to about two-fifths, and by 1945 the debt held by the public exceeded GDP. Women's employment rose almost 60 percent, a Black worker proposed a 'double victory', and the Bracero Program brought Mexican workers on labor contracts. Executive Order 9066 led to the removal of about 122,000 people of Japanese ancestry; the Court upheld the exclusion in 1944, Congress apologized in 1988, and in 2018 the Chief Justice called Korematsu 'gravely wrong the day it was decided'.
body: Measured in chained 2017 dollars, real GDP rose from $1,312 billion in 1939 to $2,525 billion in 1944, about 92 percent, before slipping to $2,500 billion in 1945 and $2,210 billion in 1946. [[c-us6-home-gdp]] Federal net outlays rose from 9.8 percent of GDP in fiscal 1939 to 40.7 percent in 1944 and 1945. Federal debt held by the public, 44.3 percent of GDP in 1939, reached 103.2 percent in 1945. [[c-us6-home-fiscal]] The Women's Bureau reported in 1946 that women's employment had 'increased almost 60 percent between 1940 and 1945'. [[c-us6-home-women]] Using new data on wartime employment and job placements, the economist Evan K. Rose argues that where women took wartime jobs was driven mainly by industrial mobilization rather than by drafted men leaving local labor markets, and that the areas most exposed to wartime work show 'limited overall effects on female labor force participation in 1950'. [[c-us6-home-rose]]

In a letter to the Pittsburgh Courier dated 31 January 1942, James G. Thompson proposed: 'let we colored Americans adopt the double VV for a double victory'. 'Locked out of jobs on the factory floor', as the National Park Service puts it, Thompson worked in the cafeteria at Cessna. [[c-us6-home-doublev]] The Bracero Program brought Mexican workers to the United States on labor contracts; from 1942 to 1964, 4.6 million contracts were signed. That is a count of contracts, not of individual workers. [[c-us6-home-bracero]] In the Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles, 3-10 June 1943, 'Many zoot-suiters were beaten by servicemen and stripped of their zoot suits on the spot.' [[c-us6-home-zoot]]

Executive Order 9066, signed on 19 February 1942, 'authorized the forced removal of all persons deemed a threat to national security'. About 122,000 people of Japanese ancestry were removed, nearly 70,000 of them American citizens, and held in ten incarceration centers. [[c-us6-home-eo9066]] On 18 December 1944, in Korematsu v. United States, the Court upheld the exclusion order by six votes to three. Writing for the Court, Justice Hugo Black said that courts 'must subject them to the most rigid scrutiny', meaning legal restrictions on a single racial group. Dissenting, Justice Frank Murphy called the decision 'this legalization of racism', and Justice Robert Jackson warned that its principle 'lies about like a loaded weapon'. [[c-us6-home-korematsu]]

The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 found that the incarceration had been 'motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership', apologized, and provided 'a $20,000 cash payment to each person who was incarcerated'. [[c-us6-home-redress]] In Trump v. Hawaii (2018), in an opinion upholding the president's travel proclamation, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote: 'Korematsu was gravely wrong the day it was decided, has been overruled in the court of history'. [[c-us6-home-hawaii]] In June 2025, under the executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History', the Interior Department and the Park Service put up signs at Manzanar and Minidoka inviting visitors to report negative content. The Japanese American National Museum said it was 'deeply disturbed by this new directive'. On 20 September 2025 The Washington Post reported that a sign about the detention of Japanese Americans had been removed at at least one more park. In June 2026 a federal district judge, Angel Kelley, ordered the administration to restore park signage removed in 2025, and KQED reported that at Manzanar QR codes had been posted asking the public what should be taken down. On 2 July 2026 the First Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that order, finding the Interior Department likely to succeed in its appeal. That is the status as of July 2026; the appeal continues. [[c-us6-home-signs]]

practice.why: Chief Justice Roberts, in an opinion that upheld the travel proclamation, wrote that Korematsu 'was gravely wrong the day it was decided, has been overruled in the court of history'.

wrong.1: Roberts wrote that it 'has been overruled in the court of history'.
wrong.2: Payments came from Congress: the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 provided $20,000 to each person incarcerated.
wrong.3: The Court upheld the proclamation.

pages.title: Americans at war
pages.lede: At Midway in June 1942 the United States lost one carrier and Japan four, and on D-Day, 6 June 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed in Normandy. The VA counts 16,112,566 Americans who served and 291,557 battle deaths, in armed forces whose segregation was not banned until 1948. In 1944 the government created the War Refugee Board but refused requests to bomb Auschwitz, and whether bombing could have saved lives is still debated.
body: At the Battle of Midway, 4-7 June 1942, the Navy's historians write, 'Against the loss of one U.S. carrier, the Japanese lost four—all of which had participated in the Pearl Harbor attack.' The American carrier lost was Yorktown. [[c-us6-war-midway]] In Europe, on D-Day, 6 June 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed by sea and air in Normandy, on beaches that included Utah and Omaha. [[c-us6-war-dday]] For the global course of the war, see 15.6.

The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 16,112,566 Americans who served in the Second World War. It lists 291,557 battle deaths, 113,842 other deaths in service and 670,846 wounded. [[c-us6-war-va]] The National WWII Museum gives slightly different totals: 407,316 killed and 671,278 wounded, plus 5,662 merchant mariners dead. [[c-us6-war-museum]] Those who served did so in segregated forces. More than one million Black men were inducted, from 2.5 million who registered, and segregation in the armed forces was not banned until President Truman's executive order of 26 July 1948. [[c-us6-war-seg]]

On the Holocaust itself, see 15.7. After a Treasury memorandum titled 'The Acquiescence of this Government in the Murder of the Jews', Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9417 on 22 January 1944. It created the War Refugee Board and made it government policy to take 'all measures within its power to rescue the victims of enemy oppression'. (The Treasury's draft had spoken of the 'immediate rescue and relief of the Jews of Europe'.) [[c-us6-war-wrb]] The Board itself claimed to have saved 'tens of thousands of lives'. [[c-us6-war-wrbsaved]] On 14 August 1944 Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy refused requests to bomb Auschwitz. Such an operation, he wrote, 'would in any case be of such doubtful efficacy that it would not warrant the use of our resources'. [[c-us6-war-mccloy]] Yet the IG Farben industrial complex next to the camp was bombed four times in the last year of the war. [[c-us6-war-farben]]

Historians disagree about what more could have been done. David S. Wyman (1984) argues, as his publisher summarizes the book, that a serious rescue effort could almost certainly have saved several hundred thousand Jews. [[c-us6-war-wyman]] William D. Rubinstein (1997) answers, as his publisher summarizes it, that few of the Jews who perished could have been saved by any Allied action. [[c-us6-war-rubinstein]] On the bombing itself, the Jewish Virtual Library notes that 'Several recent studies have suggested that it was not possible to bomb the camp', citing those of James Kitchens and Richard Levy. The same article cites Stuart Erdheim's study, which argues that bombing would have been 'no more complex than numerous other missions.' [[c-us6-war-bombing]] Richard Breitman and Allan J. Lichtman (2013) look at Roosevelt's record as a whole. As American University's news release summarizes them, they conclude that he did far more to help European Jews than any other world leader of his time. [[c-us6-war-breitman]]

practice.q: The VA and the National WWII Museum give different numbers for Americans who died in the war. What is the soundest way to use them?
choices: Cite both by source; the VA's deaths total 405,399, the Museum's 407,316
Treat the VA's 291,557 battle deaths as the full total who died in service
Conclude from both counts that the dead outnumbered the wounded
Assume the two counts differ by about 100,000, so neither is reliable
practice.why: The VA's 291,557 battle deaths and 113,842 other deaths in service sum to 405,399, close to the Museum's 407,316. The counts are close but not identical and come from different sources, so each should be attributed.

wrong.1: The VA counts a further 113,842 deaths in service outside battle.
wrong.2: The VA counts 670,846 wounded and the Museum 671,278.
wrong.3: The totals, 405,399 and 407,316, differ by fewer than 2,000.

practice.q: Which statement fits the evidence on Auschwitz?
choices: McCloy refused to bomb the camp, though the IG Farben works nearby were hit
Allied bombers struck nowhere near Auschwitz in the last year of the war
Studies of bombing are divided, and Rubinstein argues most could have been saved
The War Refugee Board, created in 1944, opposed rescue as a waste of resources
practice.why: McCloy refused the requests on 14 August 1944, while the IG Farben complex next to the camp was bombed four times in the final year of the war. Wyman and Rubinstein, among others, disagree about what rescue could have achieved.

wrong.1: The IG Farben complex next to the camp was bombed four times in the last year of the war.
wrong.2: Studies do disagree on whether the camp could have been bombed, but Rubinstein holds that few of the Jews who perished could have been saved; it is Wyman who argues that several hundred thousand could have been.
wrong.3: It was set up to take 'all measures within its power to rescue the victims of enemy oppression'.

pages.title: The atomic bomb and the end of the war
pages.lede: The Army Corps of Engineers set up the Manhattan Engineer District in 1942; the project employed 130,000 workers at its peak and tested its first bomb on 16 July 1945. Roosevelt died on 12 April; on 6 August Truman announced the bombing of Hiroshima, and Nagasaki was bombed on 9 August, with death tolls that differ by source and by the period counted. Whether the bombs were needed is still debated, and in June 1945 the United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco.
body: 'In August, the Corps set up the Manhattan Engineer District (MED) to manage the project'. Leslie Groves took charge in September 1942, and Roosevelt gave his final authorization that December. [[c-us6-bomb-med]] The project's main sites were Oak Ridge in Tennessee, Hanford in Washington and Los Alamos in New Mexico. At its peak it employed 130,000 workers, and it cost about $2.2 billion. Its first bomb was exploded in the Trinity test on 16 July 1945. [[c-us6-bomb-sites]] Roosevelt did not live to see it: he died at Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945. [[c-us6-bomb-fdr]]

On 6 August 1945 President Truman announced: 'Sixteen hours ago an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima, an important Japanese Army base.' And: 'It is an atomic bomb.' [[c-us6-bomb-truman]] A second bomb fell on Nagasaki on 9 August. [[c-us6-bomb-nagasaki]] How many died depends on who counts and over what period. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey of 1946 put the dead at between 70,000 and 80,000 in Hiroshima and over 35,000 in Nagasaki. [[c-us6-bomb-ussbs]] The Radiation Effects Research Foundation estimates 90,000 to 166,000 deaths in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki within two to four months, and says the total is 'not known precisely'. [[c-us6-bomb-rerf]] The City of Hiroshima's long-term estimate is that 237,000 people were killed directly or indirectly. [[c-us6-bomb-city]]

Was the bomb needed? Gar Alperovitz, writing in 2015, argues that American military leaders and intelligence judged Japan to be on the verge of surrender, and that the Japanese moved to surrender only after the Soviet Union entered the war: 'By and large, the top generals and admirals who managed World War II knew better.' [[c-us6-bomb-alperovitz]] Robert P. Newman (1995) holds, as the description of his book summarizes it, that Truman used the bomb to end the war as quickly and with as few casualties as possible. [[c-us6-bomb-newman]] Richard B. Frank, the author of Downfall, wrote in an H-Diplo roundtable on Hasegawa's book that anyone who could conceivably have been president in 1945 would have authorized the bombs. [[c-us6-bomb-frank]] Tsuyoshi Hasegawa (2005) writes, in a passage Frank quotes: 'The evidence is compelling that Soviet entry into the war had a strong impact on the peace party. Indeed, the Soviet attack, not the Hiroshima bomb, convinced political leaders to end the war by accepting the Potsdam Proclamation.' [[c-us6-bomb-hasegawa]]

At the San Francisco conference, from 25 April to 26 June 1945, representatives of 50 countries met. The Charter of the United Nations was signed on 26 June and came into force on 24 October 1945. [[c-us6-bomb-un]]

plate.title: Nagasaki, and was the bomb needed?

practice.q: Why do estimates of the dead at Hiroshima run from 70,000 to 237,000?
choices: They count over different periods and kinds of death, from patchy records
The higher figure combines the dead of both Hiroshima and Nagasaki
The 1946 Survey's estimate was the highest, before later downward revisions
The sources broadly agree, and the range reflects rounding alone
practice.why: The 1946 Survey made an early estimate, the RERF counts deaths within two to four months and says the total is 'not known precisely', and the city counts those killed directly or indirectly.

wrong.1: The City of Hiroshima's 237,000 is for the Hiroshima bomb alone.
wrong.2: The Survey gave 70,000 to 80,000, below the RERF's 90,000 to 166,000.
wrong.3: The estimates run from 70,000 to 237,000, and the RERF says the total is 'not known precisely'.

practice.q: Which statement would Gar Alperovitz most directly dispute?
choices: Truman used the bomb to end the war quickly and with few casualties
Japan was on the verge of surrender before the bombs were dropped
Soviet entry into the war weighed heavily in Japan's surrender
The number of dead at Hiroshima is not known with any precision
practice.why: That is Robert P. Newman's view, that Truman used the bomb to end the war as quickly and with as few casualties as possible; Alperovitz argues that Japan was on the verge of surrender and moved to surrender only after Soviet entry into the war.

wrong.1: That is Alperovitz's own argument.
wrong.2: Alperovitz argues that Japan moved to surrender only after Soviet entry, and Hasegawa writes that it had 'a strong impact on the peace party'.
wrong.3: That is the RERF's statement, not a point in this debate.
